Recyclable and Low Fat Products.title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
Recyclable and Low Fat Products.problemStatement: The Products table holds one row per product in a catalogue. Each row carries a product_id that uniquely identifies the product, plus two flag columns, low_fats and recyclable, that each store the single character 'Y' for yes or 'N' for no. There are no other values and no NULLs, so every product is definitively labelled on both dimensions. Report the product_id of every product that satisfies both flags at once: it must be low fat AND it must be recyclable. Products that satisfy only one of the two conditions, or neither, are excluded. Return a single column named product_id; each product appears at most once in the table, so no de-duplication is needed, and the rows may be returned in any order.
Recyclable and Low Fat Products.schema: Create table If Not Exists Products (product_id int, low_fats ENUM('Y', 'N'), recyclable ENUM('Y', 'N'))

solutions.name: Single WHERE Filter (two ANDed predicates)
solutions.explanation: This is a pure row-at-a-time filter: the engine scans Products, evaluates both predicates against each row independently, and emits product_id when both are true. Nothing about the answer depends on any other row, so there is no reason to involve a join, a GROUP BY or a subquery — every one of those exists to relate rows to other rows, and here rows are completely independent. Cost is one pass over the table, O(n), and it degrades to an index seek if a composite index on (low_fats, recyclable) exists. Note that the AND is genuinely restrictive: writing OR would return four of the five sample rows instead of two. The problem statement promises there are no NULLs in these two columns, so the three-valued-logic trap does not apply here — but notice that the schema above does not enforce that: `low_fats ENUM('Y','N')` is nullable, so you are relying on the problem's promise, not on the table definition. Had a NULL been present, low_fats = 'Y' would evaluate to UNKNOWN rather than true, and that row would silently drop out of the result, which is usually what you want but should still be a conscious choice.

edgeCases: No products are both low fat and recyclable.
All products are both low fat and recyclable.
The table is empty.
Recyclable and Low Fat Products.whyOneSolution: A reader coming from the join-heavy problems might try to be clever with something like product_id IN (SELECT product_id FROM Products WHERE low_fats = 'Y') combined with a second predicate, or a self-join of Products to itself on product_id, or CONCAT(low_fats, recyclable) = 'YY'. All three return the same rows but do strictly more work: the subquery and the self-join force a second pass and a matching step to re-derive a fact that already lives in the same row, and the CONCAT version wraps the columns in a function so no index can be used. When the whole test fits inside one row, the WHERE clause is the tool, and every other shape is a detour.

Find Customer Referee.title: Find Customer Referee
Find Customer Referee.problemStatement: The Customer table holds one row per customer: id identifies them, name is what they are called, and referee_id records which other customer referred them. A referee_id of NULL means nobody referred that person at all; they arrived on their own. Return the name of every customer who was not referred by the customer whose id is 2. Someone with no referee counts as not referred by 2 and must appear in the answer, which is the entire difficulty of the question: a bare referee_id <> 2 comparison silently throws those people away, because in SQL any comparison against NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN rather than TRUE, and only rows whose predicate is TRUE survive a WHERE clause. Only the name column is returned, and the rows may come back in any order.
Find Customer Referee.schema: Create table If Not Exists Customer (id int, name varchar(25), referee_id int)

solutions.name: Explicit NULL Guard in WHERE
solutions.explanation: This says out loud the two ways a customer can qualify: their referee is somebody other than 2, or they have no referee recorded. The second branch is mandatory. SQL uses three-valued logic, so for a row where referee_id is NULL the expression referee_id <> 2 is not TRUE and not FALSE but UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE, so Will, Jane and Bill would vanish without the IS NULL branch. This is the same trap that makes NOT IN dangerous: referee_id NOT IN (2) drops the NULL rows too, and a NOT IN whose subquery yields even one NULL returns no rows whatsoever. Cost-wise this is a single pass over the table with two cheap predicates, and because the column is never wrapped in a function an index on referee_id remains usable. Reach for this shape by default: it is explicit, portable, and it teaches the reader exactly where the NULLs went.

solutions.name: COALESCE the Missing Referee to a Sentinel
solutions.explanation: Instead of reasoning about UNKNOWN, this converts the unknown into a real value first. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument, so every missing referee becomes 0, and 0 <> 2 is plainly TRUE, which folds both of the previous conditions into one predicate. The mental model is different: you normalise the data before you filter it, rather than widening the filter to cope with the data. The price is that wrapping the column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable, so MySQL can no longer seek an index on referee_id and will scan; on a six row table nobody notices, on a ten million row table it matters. The sentinel must also be a value the column can never legitimately hold, which is why 0 works here for an id sequence starting at 1. Reach for it when a query has many such columns and the OR ... IS NULL branches would triple the length of the WHERE clause.

solutions.name: Anti-Join with LEFT JOIN and IS NULL
solutions.query:
SELECT c.name
FROM Customer c
LEFT JOIN Customer r
  ON r.id = c.referee_id AND r.id = 2
WHERE r.id IS NULL;
solutions.explanation: This reframes the question as set subtraction: start from all customers, try to attach the referring customer but only when that referrer is number 2, and keep the rows where the attachment failed. A LEFT JOIN preserves every left row and fills the right side with NULLs when the ON condition finds no partner, so the WHERE r.id IS NULL test is exactly 'this customer was not referred by 2'. Rows whose referee_id is NULL can never satisfy r.id = c.referee_id, so they fall into the unmatched bucket for free, with no special casing at all. It costs an extra join that the two single-table filters avoid, so it is overkill here, but it is the shape you must know: when the excluded set lives in another table, or is thousands of ids, the anti-join stays correct and fast while the tempting NOT IN (SELECT ...) version returns an empty result the moment that subquery emits a single NULL.

edgeCases: All customers have a referee_id equal to 2 (should return empty output).
The referee_id values are all NULL (should return all customers).
The referee_id is NULL for some customers and non-null (excluding 2) for others.

Big Countries.title: Big Countries
Big Countries.problemStatement: The World table holds one row per country, with its name, the continent it sits on, its area in square kilometres, its population, and its gdp. A country counts as "big" when it satisfies at least one of two independent thresholds: an area of 3,000,000 sq km or more, or a population of 25,000,000 or more. Meeting either threshold is enough; a country that meets both is still reported exactly once. Return three columns for every big country - name, population, and area, in that column order. Countries that meet neither threshold are excluded entirely. The result may be returned in any order, and no tie-breaking is needed because each country appears in the table only once.
Big Countries.schema: Create table If Not Exists World (name varchar(50), continent varchar(50), area int, population int, gdp bigint)

solutions.name: Single Scan with OR
solutions.explanation: This is the direct translation of the English rule into a predicate: one pass over World, keeping any row where either threshold holds. Each country appears only once in the table, and a WHERE clause never turns one input row into two output rows, so there is no chance of a duplicate and no DISTINCT is needed. (Whether or not the OR short-circuits is irrelevant to that - short-circuiting only decides how much of the predicate gets evaluated, never how many rows come out. Contrast a join, where one row can match several partners and duplicates are a real risk.) The cost is one full table scan: most engines cannot combine two separate single-column indexes cleanly across an OR, so an index on area and an index on population usually go unused here. Reach for this shape first - it is the clearest statement of intent, and on a table small enough that a scan is cheap, clarity wins over micro-optimisation. NULLs are not a trap here: if area were NULL the comparison yields UNKNOWN, that branch simply fails, and the population branch still gets its chance.

solutions.name: UNION of Two Index-Friendly Scans
solutions.explanation: Here the OR is decomposed into two separate range queries whose results are merged. Each branch touches exactly one column, so an index on area can drive the first branch and an index on population the second - something the optimiser often cannot arrange for a single OR predicate. The catch is that a country satisfying both thresholds is produced twice, so UNION (not UNION ALL) is essential: it de-duplicates, usually via a sort or hash, and that de-duplication is the price you pay for the index access. Reach for this shape when the table is large, the thresholds are selective, and both columns are indexed; stay with the plain OR when the table is small, because two scans plus a distinct pass can easily cost more than one straight scan.

edgeCases: Countries matching only one criteria.
Countries matching both criteria.
Countries matching neither criteria.

Article Views I.title: Article Views I
Article Views I.problemStatement: The Views table logs one row every time a person opens an article. A row records which article was opened (article_id), who wrote it (author_id), who opened it (viewer_id) and on what day (view_date). The same person can open the same article on many days, and the table has no primary key, so exact duplicate rows are possible. An author is said to have read their own work whenever a logged view has the viewer equal to the author of that article. Return the ids of every such self-viewing author, one row per author no matter how many self-views they logged, in a single column named id, sorted by id in ascending order.
Article Views I.schema: Create table If Not Exists Views (article_id int, author_id int, viewer_id int, view_date date)

solutions.name: Row Filter with DISTINCT
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT author_id AS id
FROM Views
WHERE author_id = viewer_id
ORDER BY id ASC;
solutions.explanation: The self-view condition lives entirely inside one row: author_id and viewer_id sit side by side, so no join and no grouping are needed. The WHERE clause keeps only the rows where the reader is the writer, and DISTINCT collapses the repeats that come from an author reading their own article on several days or from duplicate log rows. This is the cheapest shape available: one scan, one sort for the DISTINCT plus ORDER BY, no intermediate hash table for aggregates. Reach for it whenever the predicate you need can be evaluated from a single row's own columns, and only escalate to grouping or subqueries when the test depends on other rows.

solutions.name: GROUP BY with Conditional Aggregation
solutions.query:
SELECT author_id AS id
FROM Views
GROUP BY author_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN author_id = viewer_id THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0
ORDER BY id ASC;
solutions.explanation: Here the mental model flips: instead of filtering rows and then de-duplicating, we build one bucket per author and ask a question about the bucket. The CASE turns each row into a 1 when it is a self-view and 0 otherwise, SUM counts them, and HAVING keeps the authors whose count is above zero. GROUP BY gives the de-duplication for free, so no DISTINCT is required. It costs more than the plain filter because every row is aggregated rather than discarded early, but it is the shape to reach for the moment the requirement grows: swap the HAVING for '= 0' to find authors who never read themselves, or add COUNT(*) to report how many views each author got, neither of which the simple filter can express.

solutions.name: Semi-Join with EXISTS
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT v.author_id AS id
FROM Views v
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Views s
    WHERE s.author_id = v.author_id
      AND s.viewer_id = s.author_id
)
ORDER BY id ASC;
solutions.explanation: This treats the task as membership: keep an author if somewhere in the log there exists a row where that author viewed their own article. EXISTS is a semi-join, so the engine can stop scanning the inner side at the first match rather than counting everything, and it never multiplies the outer rows the way a plain JOIN to the same table would. Unlike NOT IN, EXISTS is completely safe around NULLs because it answers only true or false, never unknown; if this were the negative version ('authors who never viewed themselves') NOT EXISTS would be the correct tool and NOT IN over a nullable column would silently return zero rows. Prefer this shape when the condition is about the existence of a related row rather than about the current row's own values.

edgeCases: Authors viewing their own articles multiple times (handled by DISTINCT).
No authors viewed their own articles.
The table is empty.

Invalid Tweets.title: Invalid Tweets
Invalid Tweets.problemStatement: The Tweets table stores one row per posted tweet: tweet_id, which uniquely identifies the tweet, and content, the text that was posted. A tweet counts as invalid when the number of CHARACTERS in its content is strictly greater than 15 - a tweet of exactly 15 characters is still valid, so the comparison is > and not >=. Return the tweet_id of every invalid tweet, one row per tweet, with no other columns. The result may be returned in any order, and there is no tie-breaking rule to worry about because tweet_id is unique. The word 'characters' matters more than it looks: an emoji or an accented letter is one character but several bytes, so a byte-based length would mislabel short tweets as invalid.
Invalid Tweets.schema: Create table If Not Exists Tweets (tweet_id int, content varchar(50))

rows: Let us make America great again!

solutions.name: Length Filter (CHAR_LENGTH in WHERE)
solutions.explanation: One scan of the table, one predicate per row, nothing to join and nothing to group - the shape of the query mirrors the shape of the rule exactly. The only real decision is which length function to call. CHAR_LENGTH() counts characters, LENGTH() counts bytes, and in MySQL's default utf8mb4 they disagree the moment a tweet contains an emoji or an accent: 'Grüße' is 5 characters but 7 bytes, so LENGTH() would wrongly flag borderline tweets. Use CHAR_LENGTH() whenever the rule is written in terms of characters a human can see. The filter is also NULL-safe in the way SQL intends: if a content value were NULL, CHAR_LENGTH(NULL) is NULL, NULL > 15 is UNKNOWN, and the row is simply not returned - a NULL tweet is never reported as invalid.

edgeCases: Tweets with content length exactly 15 (should not be included).
Tweets with empty content (length 0).
Content containing multi-byte characters like emojis or non-English script.
Invalid Tweets.whyOneSolution: The rule is a single per-row predicate, so every other shape is the same scan in disguise. You could write LIKE '________________%' with sixteen underscores, or SUBSTRING(content, 16, 1) <> '', or swap CHAR_LENGTH for LENGTH - but the pattern version is unreadable and easy to miscount, the SUBSTRING version hides the intent, and LENGTH silently measures bytes instead of characters, which is a bug rather than an alternative. There is no set to join against and nothing to aggregate, so a subquery, EXISTS or a window function would only add work around the identical WHERE clause.

Product Sales Analysis I.title: Product Sales Analysis I
Product Sales Analysis I.problemStatement: There are two tables. Sales has one row per sale with sale_id, product_id, year, quantity and price, where the identifier of a sale is the sale_id together with the year, and price is the money that particular sale brought in. Product has one row per product with product_id and its product_name, and product_id is unique there. Every product_id appearing in Sales is guaranteed to exist in Product, but Product may also list items that were never sold. Report one row for each row of Sales, showing the human readable product_name that the sale's product_id refers to, the year of the sale, and the price of the sale. Nothing is aggregated and nothing is deduplicated: if the same product sold in two different years there are two output rows. Products that never appear in Sales contribute no rows at all. The result may be returned in any order.
Product Sales Analysis I.schema:
Create table If Not Exists Sales (sale_id int, product_id int, year int, quantity int, price int)
Create table If Not Exists Product (product_id int, product_name varchar(10))

solutions.name: Inner Join on product_id
solutions.query:
SELECT p.product_name,
       s.year,
       s.price
FROM Sales s
INNER JOIN Product p
  ON p.product_id = s.product_id;
solutions.explanation: This is the canonical shape for 'replace a foreign key with the readable thing it points at'. Sales drives the result and Product is consulted once per row through its primary key, so the output has exactly as many rows as Sales has, with the id swapped for a name. INNER is the right qualifier: it silently drops any sale whose product_id had no match, which is safe here because the constraint guarantees a match, and it also drops unsold products such as Samsung, which is what we want since the question asks about sales, not about the catalogue. If you ever suspect the guarantee is not enforced, switching INNER to LEFT preserves every sale and shows a NULL product_name instead, which is the fastest way to spot orphaned foreign keys during debugging.

solutions.name: Correlated Scalar Subquery Lookup
solutions.query:
SELECT (SELECT p.product_name
        FROM Product p
        WHERE p.product_id = s.product_id) AS product_name,
       s.year,
       s.price
FROM Sales s;
solutions.explanation: Instead of joining, the query stays anchored on Sales and performs a point lookup in the select list, which is the mental model of 'dereference a pointer' rather than 'combine two sets'. It is guaranteed not to change the row count no matter what Product contains, which is its real advantage: a join against a table whose key was accidentally duplicated would quietly multiply rows, whereas a scalar subquery would raise an error instead of lying. Its NULL behaviour is that of a LEFT JOIN, since a lookup that finds nothing yields NULL rather than removing the sale. The cost is one indexed probe per Sales row and the fact that it can only produce one column per subquery, so needing three fields from Product would mean three lookups and a real join becomes the better tool.

edgeCases: Products that exist in the Product table but have no matching entries in the Sales table (handled by INNER JOIN which omits them).
Multiple sales of the same product in the same year or in different years.

Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make An.title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make An.problemStatement: Two tables describe activity in a shop. Visits has one row per visit: visit_id is the primary key and customer_id says who walked in. Transactions has one row per purchase made during a visit: transaction_id is the primary key, visit_id points back at the visit it happened during, and amount is how much was spent. A single visit can produce several transactions, or none at all, and a visit_id present in Visits may be entirely absent from Transactions. Find the customers who came in and left without buying anything, and say how often that happened to them. For each customer who has at least one such empty-handed visit, return customer_id together with count_no_trans, the number of that customer's visits that generated zero transactions. Customers whose every visit produced a purchase must not appear at all. Any row order is accepted.
Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make An.schema:
Create table If Not Exists Visits (visit_id int, customer_id int)
Create table If Not Exists Transactions (transaction_id int, visit_id int, amount int)

solutions.name: LEFT JOIN Anti-Join (IS NULL filter)
solutions.query:
SELECT v.customer_id, COUNT(v.visit_id) AS count_no_trans
FROM Visits v
LEFT JOIN Transactions t ON v.visit_id = t.visit_id
WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL
GROUP BY v.customer_id;
solutions.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps every visit, matched or not, and manufactures a row of NULLs on the Transactions side whenever a visit has no purchase. Filtering on t.transaction_id IS NULL after the join therefore keeps exactly the unmatched visits — the classic anti-join. Two details make it correct: the IS NULL test must sit in WHERE, not in the ON clause (in ON it would change which rows match rather than filter the joined result), and the column tested must be one that can never be NULL in a real matched row, so transaction_id, the primary key, is the safe choice. Each surviving row is one empty visit, so COUNT after GROUP BY customer_id counts visits, not transactions. Reach for this shape when the optimiser has good join support and you may also want columns from the right table; the cost is that the engine materialises matches before throwing them away, so a customer with a hundred purchases per visit still has those hundred rows built and discarded.

solutions.name: NOT IN Subquery
solutions.query:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(visit_id) AS count_no_trans
FROM Visits
WHERE visit_id NOT IN (SELECT visit_id FROM Transactions)
GROUP BY customer_id;
solutions.explanation: This reads the way the question is phrased: keep the visits whose id never shows up in Transactions, then count them per customer. The subquery is uncorrelated, so MySQL evaluates it once and probes an in-memory set for each visit, which is cheap. The trap worth memorising is NULL: NOT IN is evaluated as a chain of <> comparisons, and comparing anything to NULL yields UNKNOWN rather than true, so if Transactions.visit_id contained a single NULL this query would return zero rows for every customer — silently, with no error. Here visit_id is a non-nullable foreign key so it is safe, but the habit to build is either to add WHERE visit_id IS NOT NULL inside the subquery or to prefer NOT EXISTS. Use NOT IN when the inner column is provably non-nullable and the list is small enough to hash.

solutions.name: NOT EXISTS Correlated Subquery
solutions.explanation: NOT EXISTS states the requirement directly: for this visit, no transaction row exists. The subquery is correlated, so conceptually it runs per visit, but it can stop at the first match instead of building a full result — SELECT 1 makes it explicit that the projected value is irrelevant, only the presence of a row matters. Unlike NOT IN this form is immune to NULLs: a NULL visit_id inside Transactions simply fails the equality and never counts as a match, so the answer stays correct instead of collapsing to nothing. Compared with the LEFT JOIN it never materialises the matched rows it is about to discard, which matters when a visit has many transactions. Reach for NOT EXISTS as the default anti-join in production code: it is the most readable of the three, the most robust to NULLs, and optimisers generally rewrite it into the same anti-join plan as the LEFT JOIN version.

edgeCases: Multiple transactions made in a single visit (the LEFT JOIN approach ensures we count only visits without any transaction).
All customers made transactions (should return empty output).
No customer made transactions.

Rising Temperature.title: Rising Temperature
Rising Temperature.problemStatement: The Weather table stores one reading per calendar day: id is an arbitrary identifier for the reading, recordDate is the day it was taken, and temperature is the value recorded. Dates are unique but the ids are not guaranteed to run in date order, and the calendar may have holes where a day was never recorded. Return the id of every day whose temperature is strictly greater than the temperature of the day immediately before it, meaning exactly one calendar day earlier. Comparison is against yesterday's actual date, not against whichever earlier reading happens to be nearest, so a day sitting just after a gap has nothing to compare with and is never reported. The first recorded day is likewise excluded, equal temperatures do not count, only the id column is returned, and the rows may be in any order.
Rising Temperature.schema: Create table If Not Exists Weather (id int, recordDate date, temperature int)

solutions.name: Self-Join on Consecutive Dates
solutions.query:
SELECT w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2
  ON DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;
solutions.explanation: The table is joined to itself so that one copy plays the role of today (w1) and the other plays yesterday (w2), paired by DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1, which is true only when w1 is exactly one day after w2. Once the rows are side by side, the comparison is an ordinary WHERE test. The inner join is doing the exclusion work for free: a day with no reading for the previous date simply finds no partner and disappears, so the first day and any day after a calendar gap never reach the WHERE clause. The catch is performance. Because the join predicate wraps recordDate in a function, MySQL cannot use an index on it and evaluates something close to a nested loop over every pair; writing the equivalent w2.recordDate = w1.recordDate - INTERVAL 1 DAY keeps the index seekable on w2. Reach for the self-join when the comparison is against a specific, computable key rather than against 'the previous row', which is what makes it read so naturally here.

solutions.name: Correlated Scalar Subquery
solutions.query:
SELECT w.id
FROM Weather w
WHERE w.temperature > (
    SELECT w2.temperature
    FROM Weather w2
    WHERE DATEDIFF(w.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1
);
solutions.explanation: Here the mental model is row by row rather than set against set: for each day, go and look up yesterday's temperature, then compare. The subquery is correlated because it mentions w.recordDate from the outer row, so it is conceptually re-evaluated once per day and must return at most one value, which holds because recordDate is unique. NULL behaviour is what makes this version work without an extra guard: when yesterday has no reading the subquery returns NULL, the comparison temperature > NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN instead of TRUE, and the row is quietly dropped, which is precisely the rule we want. The cost is that the optimiser often executes it as one lookup per outer row, so it can be slower than the join on large tables. Reach for it when you want one scalar fact about a related row and dragging that whole row into the FROM clause would obscure the intent.

solutions.name: LAG Window Function
solutions.query:
SELECT id
FROM (
    SELECT id,
           recordDate,
           temperature,
           LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp,
           LAG(recordDate)  OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_date
    FROM Weather
) t
WHERE temperature > prev_temp
  AND DATEDIFF(recordDate, prev_date) = 1;
solutions.explanation: This treats the table as an ordered sequence. Sorting by recordDate inside the OVER clause, LAG pulls the previous row's temperature and date onto the current row, turning a comparison between two rows into a comparison between two columns of one row. Note carefully that LAG gives the previous existing reading, not literally yesterday, so the DATEDIFF check is still required: without it a day sitting after a two week gap would be compared against the reading before the gap and wrongly reported. On the very first row LAG returns NULL, and both predicates then evaluate to UNKNOWN, so that row is filtered out with no special handling. Cost is one sort of the table rather than a join, which is usually the cheapest of the three, and the shape scales: asking for a three day rise, or a per-city rise via PARTITION BY city, is a small edit here but another join in the first version.

edgeCases: Non-consecutive dates in the database (e.g. gaps of a few days - DATEDIFF condition handles this and returns only consecutive day rises).
Equal temperatures on consecutive days (should not be included).
Temperature rises but dates are out of order in the database (handled properly by the join condition).

Average Time of Process per Machine.title: Average Time of Process per Machine
Average Time of Process per Machine.problemStatement: The Activity table logs machine events. Each row records a machine_id, a process_id, an activity_type that is either 'start' or 'end', and a floating-point timestamp in seconds. Every process running on a machine contributes exactly two rows - one 'start' and one matching 'end' with the same machine_id and process_id - and the 'end' timestamp is always greater than the 'start' timestamp. A process is identified only within its machine, so process_id 0 on machine 0 is a different process from process_id 0 on machine 1. For each machine, report machine_id and processing_time, where processing_time is the total time spent across all of that machine's processes divided by the number of processes on that machine, rounded to 3 decimal places. Every machine in the table appears in the output; the rows may be returned in any order.
Average Time of Process per Machine.schema: Create table If Not Exists Activity (machine_id int, process_id int, activity_type ENUM('start', 'end'), timestamp float)

solutions.name: Self Join of Start Rows to End Rows
solutions.query:
SELECT a1.machine_id, ROUND(AVG(a2.timestamp - a1.timestamp), 3) AS processing_time
FROM Activity a1
JOIN Activity a2
  ON a1.machine_id = a2.machine_id
 AND a1.process_id = a2.process_id
 AND a1.activity_type = 'start'
 AND a2.activity_type = 'end'
GROUP BY a1.machine_id;
solutions.explanation: The table stores one event per row, but the quantity we want lives across two rows, so the join reassembles each process into a single row: a1 is pinned to the 'start' event and a2 to the matching 'end' event on the same machine and process. Once the pair is on one row, the duration is plain subtraction and AVG over the group does the rest - no explicit divide, because AVG already counts exactly one joined row per process. This is the shape to reach for when the pairing rule is the interesting part, since it reads almost like the problem statement. Its cost is that Activity is read twice and joined; with an index on (machine_id, process_id, activity_type) that is cheap, without one it is a hash join over the whole table. Note that the activity_type predicates belong in the ON clause here precisely because it is an inner join - a process missing its 'end' row simply drops out rather than producing a NULL duration.

solutions.name: Conditional Aggregation in One Pass
solutions.query:
SELECT machine_id,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN activity_type = 'end' THEN timestamp ELSE -timestamp END)
             / COUNT(DISTINCT process_id), 3) AS processing_time
FROM Activity
GROUP BY machine_id;
solutions.explanation: This drops the join entirely by exploiting an algebraic fact: the sum of all durations equals the sum of every 'end' timestamp minus the sum of every 'start' timestamp, so signing each row by its activity_type and adding them up gives the total elapsed time per machine in a single scan. Dividing by COUNT(DISTINCT process_id) turns that total into the required average. It is the cheapest plan available - one pass, one grouping, no second read of the table - and it is the pattern to learn for any problem where paired rows only ever need to be summed rather than examined individually. The trade-offs are real, though: it silently assumes every process is perfectly paired, since an orphan 'start' would quietly deflate the total, and it cannot express anything per-process such as a maximum duration. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) also ignores NULL process_ids, which is the correct behaviour here but worth knowing.

solutions.name: Correlated Subquery Pulling the End Timestamp
solutions.query:
SELECT machine_id, ROUND(AVG(duration), 3) AS processing_time
FROM (
    SELECT a.machine_id,
           (SELECT e.timestamp
            FROM Activity e
            WHERE e.machine_id = a.machine_id
              AND e.process_id = a.process_id
              AND e.activity_type = 'end') - a.timestamp AS duration
    FROM Activity a
    WHERE a.activity_type = 'start'
) t
GROUP BY machine_id;
solutions.explanation: Instead of joining two row sets, this walks the 'start' rows and, for each one, looks up its partner 'end' timestamp with a correlated scalar subquery, so the duration is computed row by row before any grouping happens. The mental model is a lookup rather than a set match, which is often the easier one to hold when only a single column has to be fetched from the other side. The cost is the flip side of that: conceptually the subquery re-executes once per 'start' row, so without an index on (machine_id, process_id, activity_type) it degrades badly on large tables, whereas the self join can be planned as one hash pass. It is also the shape that fails loudest on bad data - a process with no 'end' row yields NULL for that duration, and AVG then skips it rather than counting it as zero, which is usually what you want but is worth stating out loud.

edgeCases: Varying number of processes per machine.
Timestamps with high precision float values (handled by ROUND).

Employee Bonus.title: Employee Bonus
Employee Bonus.problemStatement: Two tables describe a small company. Employee holds one row per person with their id (empId), name, the empId of their supervisor and their salary; supervisor may be NULL for someone at the top. Bonus holds at most one row per employee, keyed by empId, recording the bonus that person was awarded; employees who received no bonus simply have no row in Bonus at all. Report the name of every employee whose bonus is strictly less than 1000, and treat an employee with no bonus record as qualifying too, since receiving nothing is less than 1000. Each output row is the employee's name together with their bonus, which must come back as NULL for anyone missing from Bonus. The result may be returned in any order.
Employee Bonus.schema:
Create table If Not Exists Employee (empId int, name varchar(255), supervisor int, salary int)
Create table If Not Exists Bonus (empId int, bonus int)

solutions.name: LEFT JOIN with a NULL-Aware Filter
solutions.query:
SELECT e.name, b.bonus
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId
WHERE b.bonus < 1000 OR b.bonus IS NULL;
solutions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every employee and attaches the bonus row when one exists, filling b.bonus with NULL when it does not. The filter then has to handle both populations explicitly, and this is where the classic trap lives: the comparison 'NULL < 1000' evaluates to unknown, not true, so a bare 'WHERE b.bonus < 1000' would silently throw away exactly the bonus-less employees the question wants. Adding 'OR b.bonus IS NULL' restores them. One pass over each table plus a hash or index lookup on empId makes this the cheapest shape, and it is the default choice whenever you need every row of the left table plus optional detail from the right.

solutions.name: Correlated Scalar Subquery
solutions.explanation: Rather than joining, this drives off Employee and looks the bonus up per row. A scalar subquery that finds nothing yields NULL, which reproduces the LEFT JOIN's behaviour without writing a join at all, and IFNULL turns that missing value into 0 in the filter so the three-valued-logic problem never arises. It only works because empId is unique in Bonus; if a second bonus row existed for the same employee the subquery would raise a cardinality error instead of quietly duplicating rows, which is either a safety feature or an annoyance depending on your data. The cost is that the lookup can run twice per employee unless the optimiser folds it, so prefer the LEFT JOIN on large tables and reach for this when you want one optional attribute and find the join-plus-NULL-filter harder to read.

solutions.name: UNION ALL of Two Disjoint Cases
solutions.query:
SELECT e.name, b.bonus
FROM Employee e
JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId
WHERE b.bonus < 1000
UNION ALL
SELECT e.name, NULL AS bonus
FROM Employee e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Bonus b WHERE b.empId = e.empId);
solutions.explanation: This spells out the two populations the question quietly merges: employees who have a small bonus, found with an ordinary inner join, and employees who have no bonus row at all, found with an anti-join via NOT EXISTS. Because the two branches are provably disjoint, UNION ALL is correct and avoids the de-duplication sort that plain UNION would impose. The payoff is clarity — nobody reading it can miss that missing bonuses are deliberately included, and the literal NULL in the second branch documents the output shape. The cost is two scans of Employee. Note that NOT EXISTS is the safe anti-join here; 'empId NOT IN (SELECT empId FROM Bonus)' would return no rows at all if Bonus ever contained a NULL empId, since NULL makes every NOT IN comparison unknown.

edgeCases: Employees who do not have a record in the Bonus table (their bonus is NULL, which must be included).
Employees with a bonus of exactly 1000 (should be excluded).
All employees have bonuses >= 1000.

Students and Examinations.title: Students and Examinations
Students and Examinations.problemStatement: Three tables describe a school. Students holds one row per student (student_id, student_name). Subjects holds one row per subject taught (subject_name). Examinations holds one row for every sitting: a student_id and a subject_name recorded each time that student took that exam, so the same pair can appear many times and the table has no primary key. Report one row for EVERY combination of student and subject - all students crossed with all subjects, whether or not the exam was ever taken - with columns student_id, student_name, subject_name and attended_exams, the number of times that student sat that subject. Combinations that never appear in Examinations must still be listed with attended_exams = 0. Order the result by student_id, then by subject_name.
Students and Examinations.schema:
Create table If Not Exists Students (student_id int, student_name varchar(20))
Create table If Not Exists Subjects (subject_name varchar(20))
Create table If Not Exists Examinations (student_id int, subject_name varchar(20))

solutions.name: CROSS JOIN Grid + LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY
solutions.query:
SELECT s.student_id,
       s.student_name,
       sub.subject_name,
       COUNT(e.subject_name) AS attended_exams
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Subjects sub
LEFT JOIN Examinations e
       ON e.student_id = s.student_id
      AND e.subject_name = sub.subject_name
GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name
ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;
solutions.explanation: The trap in this question is that grouping Examinations alone can never produce the zero rows - a student who skipped Physics has no Physics row to group. So you first MANUFACTURE the rows you are required to report: Students CROSS JOIN Subjects is every student-subject pair, the complete grid the answer must cover. Only then do you LEFT JOIN the sittings onto that grid, which keeps the grid intact and attaches NULLs where nothing matched. The last subtlety is COUNT(e.subject_name) rather than COUNT(*): COUNT of a column ignores NULLs, so an unmatched grid cell counts 0, whereas COUNT(*) counts the single NULL-padded row and would wrongly report 1. This is the default shape whenever a report must show 'every category, including the empty ones'.

solutions.name: Correlated Scalar Subquery per Grid Cell
solutions.query:
SELECT s.student_id
     , s.student_name
     , sub.subject_name
     , (SELECT COUNT(*)
          FROM Examinations e
         WHERE e.student_id = s.student_id
           AND e.subject_name = sub.subject_name) AS attended_exams
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Subjects sub
ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;
solutions.explanation: Same grid, different way of filling it in. Instead of joining and then collapsing with GROUP BY, you build the grid and ask a counting question once per cell. The mental model is a spreadsheet formula: for this student and this subject, how many sittings exist? Because a correlated COUNT over zero matching rows returns 0 rather than NULL, the empty cells come out right with no COALESCE and no COUNT-the-right-column subtlety - that is the readability win over the LEFT JOIN version. The cost is that the subquery is evaluated per output row, so without an index on Examinations(student_id, subject_name) it degrades to students x subjects scans of the sittings table. Prefer it for small dimension tables or when you need several independent per-cell metrics that would otherwise fight over one GROUP BY.

solutions.name: Pre-aggregate in a CTE, then LEFT JOIN the Counts
solutions.query:
WITH exam_counts AS (
    SELECT student_id, subject_name, COUNT(*) AS attended
    FROM Examinations
    GROUP BY student_id, subject_name
)
SELECT s.student_id,
       s.student_name,
       sub.subject_name,
       COALESCE(c.attended, 0) AS attended_exams
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Subjects sub
LEFT JOIN exam_counts c
       ON c.student_id = s.student_id
      AND c.subject_name = sub.subject_name
ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;
solutions.explanation: Aggregate first, join second. The CTE reduces Examinations to at most one row per student-subject pair, and the outer query simply decorates the grid with those pre-computed numbers, turning the missing ones into 0 with COALESCE. Two things make this worth knowing. First, the join is now one-to-one, so the outer query needs no GROUP BY - which means you can safely add more columns from Students without having to list them in a grouping clause, the mistake that breaks the first approach for beginners. Second, it scales: joining a large fact table row-by-row and grouping afterwards multiplies rows before shrinking them, while grouping first shrinks the fact table once and joins a small result. Remember COALESCE - an unmatched LEFT JOIN yields NULL, not 0, and NULL would fail the expected output.

edgeCases: Students who have not attended any exams (attended_exams should show 0 for all subjects).
Subjects that no student has taken.
Ensuring proper ordering of output by student_id and subject_name.

Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports.title: Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports
Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports.problemStatement: One table, Employee, with columns id, name, department and managerId. A row is a single person: id is their unique identifier and managerId is the id of the person they report to directly, or NULL when they report to nobody. Managers are ordinary rows in the same table, which is what makes this a self-referencing hierarchy. Report the name of every employee who is the direct manager of five or more other employees. Only direct reports count, so someone whose reports each manage large teams of their own does not accumulate those grandchildren toward the total. People with fewer than five direct reports, and people who manage nobody at all, are excluded. Each qualifying manager is reported once, and the rows may come back in any order.
Managers with at Least 5 Direct Reports.schema: Create table If Not Exists Employee (id int, name varchar(255), department varchar(255), managerId int)

solutions.name: IN a Grouped Subquery of Manager Ids
solutions.query:
SELECT name
FROM Employee
WHERE id IN (
    SELECT managerId
    FROM Employee
    GROUP BY managerId
    HAVING COUNT(id) >= 5
);
solutions.explanation: The subquery answers a smaller question on its own: group the workforce by who they report to and keep the manager ids whose bucket holds at least five people. The outer query then turns those ids back into names by looking them up in the same table. Splitting it this way keeps the counting and the naming apart, which is why it reads so cleanly. The NULL managerId rows form their own group, but that group's id can never equal any real employee id, so it harmlessly fails the IN test. Be aware that the mirror form is a trap: had the requirement been 'managers with fewer than five reports' and you reached for NOT IN over this same subquery, the NULL group would make the whole predicate UNKNOWN and the query would return zero rows.

solutions.name: Self Join with GROUP BY and HAVING
solutions.query:
SELECT e1.name
FROM Employee e1
JOIN Employee e2
  ON e2.managerId = e1.id
GROUP BY e1.id, e1.name
HAVING COUNT(e2.id) >= 5;
solutions.explanation: Here the table is joined to itself so that each output row of the join is one manager paired with one of their reports; the inner join automatically discards employees who manage nobody, because they find no partner. Grouping by the manager's id then counting the partners gives the team size directly, and HAVING filters after aggregation the way WHERE never could. Grouping on id as well as name matters: two different people could share a name, and grouping on name alone would merge their teams and manufacture a false manager. This is the shape to prefer when you also want to report something about the reports themselves, for example the team size or the list of report names, since those columns are already in scope.

solutions.name: Correlated COUNT Subquery
solutions.query:
SELECT e.name
FROM Employee e
WHERE (
    SELECT COUNT(*)
    FROM Employee r
    WHERE r.managerId = e.id
) >= 5;
solutions.explanation: This version never groups anything. It walks the employee list one row at a time and asks, for this person, how many rows point at them as manager, keeping the row when the answer reaches five. It is the most literal translation of the sentence, and because there is no GROUP BY there is no risk of collapsing two same-named people into one bucket, and no need to remember HAVING at all. COUNT(*) of an empty set is 0 rather than NULL, so employees who manage nobody are rejected cleanly rather than producing an UNKNOWN comparison. The trade is cost: the inner count is conceptually re-run per outer row, so it wants an index on managerId, whereas the grouped forms compute all the counts in a single pass and scale better on a large table.

edgeCases: A manager has exactly 5 direct reports.
A manager has fewer than 5 direct reports (should not be included).
An employee is their own manager (if cycle exists, but standard constraint avoids this).

Confirmation Rate.title: Confirmation Rate
Confirmation Rate.problemStatement: Signups has one row per registered user: user_id is the primary key and time_stamp is when they signed up. Confirmations has one row per confirmation message that was requested by a user; user_id is a foreign key into Signups, time_stamp is when the request was made, and action is either 'confirmed' or 'timeout' depending on how the user responded. A user may request many confirmations, or none at all. For every user in Signups report a confirmation rate: the number of their requests whose action is 'confirmed' divided by the total number of requests they made. A user with no rows in Confirmations has a rate of 0 rather than a NULL or a missing row, so all signed-up users must appear exactly once. Round each rate to two decimal places. Return user_id and confirmation_rate in any order.
Confirmation Rate.schema:
Create table If Not Exists Signups (user_id int, time_stamp datetime)
Create table If Not Exists Confirmations (user_id int, time_stamp datetime, action ENUM('confirmed', 'timeout'))

solutions.name: LEFT JOIN with Conditional Aggregation (SUM / COUNT)
solutions.query:
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(IFNULL(SUM(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0
                    / NULLIF(COUNT(c.action), 0), 0), 2) AS confirmation_rate
FROM Signups s
LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON c.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id;
solutions.explanation: This spells the definition out literally: the numerator is a conditional SUM that adds 1 for each 'confirmed' row, the denominator is COUNT(c.action), which counts only non-NULL actions and therefore only real requests. The LEFT JOIN is what guarantees every signed-up user reaches the output even with no confirmations; an INNER JOIN would silently drop user 6. Two guards handle that no-request group: NULLIF turns a denominator of 0 into NULL so the division yields NULL instead of a divide-by-zero, and IFNULL then converts that NULL to 0. The * 1.0 forces floating-point division — without it, integer division would turn 1/2 into 0 in several engines. Reach for this shape when you want the ratio's two halves visible and auditable, or when the numerator condition is more complicated than a single equality.

solutions.name: LEFT JOIN with AVG of a Boolean
solutions.query:
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(IFNULL(AVG(c.action = 'confirmed'), 0), 2) AS confirmation_rate
FROM Signups s
LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id;
solutions.explanation: MySQL evaluates a comparison to the integer 1 or 0, so c.action = 'confirmed' becomes a column of ones and zeros and its average is precisely the fraction that are confirmed — the numerator and denominator of the previous solution collapse into one aggregate. The NULL behaviour is the interesting part and it works in our favour twice: for a user with no confirmations the LEFT JOIN supplies NULL for c.action, NULL = 'confirmed' is NULL rather than 0, AVG ignores NULLs entirely, and the group's average is NULL, which IFNULL rewrites to 0. Had the expression produced 0 instead of NULL, that user would have contributed a phantom request. This is the shortest correct answer and the one to reach for in an interview, but it leans on MySQL's boolean-as-integer rule, so it is not portable to PostgreSQL without an explicit CASE or a cast.

solutions.name: Correlated Scalar Subquery per User
solutions.query:
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(IFNULL((SELECT AVG(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END)
                     FROM Confirmations c
                     WHERE c.user_id = s.user_id), 0), 2) AS confirmation_rate
FROM Signups s;
solutions.explanation: Here there is no join and no GROUP BY at all: the driving table is Signups, one output row per user is guaranteed structurally, and the rate is computed by a scalar subquery that aggregates that user's own confirmation rows. An aggregate over an empty set returns NULL, so a user with no requests naturally produces NULL and IFNULL turns it into 0 — the same outcome the LEFT JOIN reached, but arrived at through the subquery rather than through outer-join padding. The explicit 1.0 / 0.0 in the CASE keeps the arithmetic in floating point. The cost is that the subquery is logically re-executed for every signed-up user, so with millions of users and no index on Confirmations.user_id this is far slower than the grouped join. Reach for it when you need several independent per-user metrics with different filters and a single GROUP BY would get tangled, or when you want the outer row list to be obviously fixed.

edgeCases: User has signed up but has zero confirmation requests (handled by IFNULL to return 0.00).
User has only 'timeout' actions (rate is 0.00).
User has only 'confirmed' actions (rate is 1.00).

Not Boring Movies.title: Not Boring Movies
Not Boring Movies.problemStatement: The Cinema table holds one row per movie: id is its numeric identifier, movie is the title, description is a short blurb, and rating is a floating point score. Return every column of the rows for movies that satisfy two conditions at once, namely that the id is an odd number and that the description is not exactly the word 'boring'. Movies whose id is even are excluded no matter how good they are, and a movie described as boring is excluded even when its id is odd. The surviving rows are sorted by rating from highest to lowest, so the best film appears first. The question does not define a tie-break for two movies with the same rating, so any order among equals is accepted.
Not Boring Movies.schema: Create table If Not Exists Cinema (id int, movie varchar(255), description varchar(255), rating float)

solutions.name: Direct Filter with ORDER BY
solutions.query:
SELECT id, movie, description, rating
FROM Cinema
WHERE id % 2 = 1
  AND description <> 'boring'
ORDER BY rating DESC;
solutions.explanation: Both requirements are properties of a single row, so both belong in the WHERE clause and the engine can decide each row's fate in one pass, then sort what survives. id % 2 = 1 keeps odd identifiers; since ids here are positive this is safe, though in engines where the modulo of a negative number is negative you would write ABS(id) % 2 = 1 to stay honest. description <> 'boring' does the second cut, and two details are worth knowing: under MySQL's default case-insensitive collation this also removes a description of 'Boring', and if any description were NULL the comparison would evaluate to UNKNOWN and that movie would be dropped, so a data set with missing blurbs needs OR description IS NULL. ORDER BY rating DESC is applied after filtering, which is why the answer is ranked best first. The whole plan is one scan plus one sort, with no join or aggregation to reason about.

edgeCases: Movies with even IDs and non-boring descriptions (should be excluded).
Movies with odd IDs and boring descriptions (should be excluded).
All movies are boring or have even IDs (should return empty result).
Not Boring Movies.whyOneSolution: A reader might reach for MOD(id, 2) = 1, id & 1 = 1, or an id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM Cinema WHERE id % 2 = 0) subquery, but none of those is a different way of thinking about the problem: there is no join, no grouping and no cross-row context here, just one scan of one table with a two part row predicate and a sort. Those variants only re-spell how parity is tested, and the subquery version is strictly worse because it reads the table twice to answer a question each row can answer about itself.

Average Selling Price.title: Average Selling Price
Average Selling Price.problemStatement: Two tables describe a catalogue. Prices holds non-overlapping price periods: each row says that product_id carried price (a whole number of currency units) on every date from start_date through end_date inclusive. UnitsSold holds sales events: each row says that units of product_id were bought on purchase_date. A sale is priced by finding the Prices row for the same product whose date window contains the purchase_date. For every product that appears in Prices, report product_id and average_price, where average_price is total revenue - the sum over all of that product's sales of units multiplied by the price in force that day - divided by the total number of units sold, rounded to 2 decimal places. A product with no sales at all must still appear, with an average_price of 0 rather than being dropped or reported as NULL. Rows may come back in any order.
Average Selling Price.schema:
Create table If Not Exists Prices (product_id int, start_date date, end_date date, price int)
Create table If Not Exists UnitsSold (product_id int, purchase_date date, units int)

solutions.name: LEFT JOIN with Weighted Aggregation
solutions.query:
SELECT p.product_id,
       ROUND(IFNULL(SUM(u.units * p.price) / SUM(u.units), 0), 2) AS average_price
FROM Prices p
LEFT JOIN UnitsSold u
  ON p.product_id = u.product_id
 AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date
GROUP BY p.product_id;
solutions.explanation: The join condition does two jobs at once: it matches product to product and it picks the single price window that contains the purchase date, so each surviving row is one sale already carrying its correct unit price. Grouping by product then turns that into a weighted mean - revenue over units - which is the whole point, since a plain AVG(price) would treat a one-unit sale and a thousand-unit sale as equals. LEFT JOIN is what keeps product 3 alive: with no matching sale it contributes a single row of NULLs, SUM over nothing but NULL is NULL, and IFNULL converts that to the required 0. Reach for this shape by default - it is one pass over each table and the optimiser can plan it well. The subtlety to internalise is that the date predicate must live in the ON clause; move it to WHERE and the LEFT JOIN collapses into an inner join, silently deleting every product that never sold.

solutions.name: Pre-Aggregate in a CTE, Then Attach
solutions.query:
WITH sales AS (
    SELECT p.product_id,
           SUM(u.units * p.price) AS revenue,
           SUM(u.units) AS qty
    FROM Prices p
    JOIN UnitsSold u
      ON p.product_id = u.product_id
     AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date
    GROUP BY p.product_id
)
SELECT d.product_id,
       ROUND(COALESCE(s.revenue / s.qty, 0), 2) AS average_price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Prices) d
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.product_id = d.product_id;
solutions.explanation: This separates the two responsibilities that the single-query version fuses together. The CTE answers only the arithmetic question with a plain inner join - which products sold, and what revenue and quantity did they accumulate - and the outer query answers only the completeness question by starting from the full list of products and attaching those totals. Products with no sales never enter the CTE at all, so the LEFT JOIN hands them a NULL revenue and COALESCE supplies the 0. It costs an extra materialisation of the aggregate, but it is far easier to debug, because you can run the CTE alone and see the raw revenue and quantity per product before any rounding hides them. Reach for it when the grouped calculation grows past one or two expressions, or when the same aggregate has to be reused, and prefer the single LEFT JOIN when the query is small enough to read in one glance.

solutions.name: Correlated Subqueries Over a Priced-Sales CTE
solutions.query:
WITH matched AS (
    SELECT p.product_id, u.units, p.price
    FROM Prices p
    JOIN UnitsSold u
      ON p.product_id = u.product_id
     AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date
)
SELECT d.product_id,
       ROUND(COALESCE(
           (SELECT SUM(m.units * m.price) FROM matched m WHERE m.product_id = d.product_id)
           / (SELECT SUM(m.units) FROM matched m WHERE m.product_id = d.product_id), 0), 2) AS average_price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Prices) d;
solutions.explanation: Here the driving row set is simply the list of products, and each output row pulls its own numerator and denominator with correlated scalar subqueries against a CTE of already-priced sales. Nothing is grouped in the outer query at all, which is the appeal: the shape scales naturally when you want to bolt on more independent per-product figures, each as its own subquery, without worrying about how a growing GROUP BY interacts with them. The price is repeated work - conceptually two lookups per product - so on a large catalogue the pre-aggregated version wins comfortably. The NULL behaviour is the crux and repays study: for a product with no sales both subqueries return NULL, NULL divided by NULL is NULL rather than an error or a division-by-zero, and COALESCE turns that single NULL into the 0 the specification demands.

edgeCases: A product in Prices has no sales records in UnitsSold (should return average_price 0.00).
The purchase date falls exactly on the start_date or end_date (handled correctly by BETWEEN which is inclusive).

Project Employees I.title: Project Employees I
Project Employees I.problemStatement: Project is a link table: each row pairs a project_id with the employee_id of someone assigned to it, and the pair together is the primary key, so an employee appears at most once per project but may work on several projects. Employee holds one row per person with their employee_id, name and experience_years. For every project that appears in Project, compute the average experience_years across the employees assigned to it and return two columns, project_id and average_years, with the average rounded to two decimal places. An employee working on two projects contributes their experience to both averages. The result may be returned in any order.

solutions.name: JOIN then GROUP BY with AVG
solutions.query:
SELECT p.project_id,
       ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years), 2) AS average_years
FROM Project p
LEFT JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id
GROUP BY p.project_id;
solutions.explanation: The assignment rows carry no experience figure, so the first move is to join each assignment to the employee it names and pull experience_years alongside it. Once every row is a (project, experience) pair, GROUP BY project_id collapses them into one bucket per project and AVG does the arithmetic; ROUND trims the result to two decimals as asked. AVG ignores NULLs, so the LEFT JOIN is a defensive choice: an assignment pointing at a missing employee would still keep its project in the output rather than dropping it entirely, though its NULL experience would not drag the average down. This join-then-aggregate shape is the default for 'summarise a child table by a parent key' and costs one hash join plus one grouping pass.

solutions.name: Manual SUM over COUNT
solutions.query:
SELECT p.project_id,
       ROUND(SUM(e.experience_years) * 1.0 / COUNT(e.employee_id), 2) AS average_years
FROM Project p
JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id
GROUP BY p.project_id;
solutions.explanation: AVG is only shorthand for a sum divided by a count, and writing it out makes two things explicit that AVG hides. First, the multiplication by 1.0 forces floating point division; with two integer columns MySQL's AVG would still return a decimal, but the same expression written as SUM/COUNT in a strictly integer dialect would truncate, and this is exactly the bug that produces a suspiciously round answer. Second, counting e.employee_id rather than * shows that rows with no matching employee are excluded from the denominator, which is precisely what AVG does silently. Reach for the manual form when the denominator is not simply 'the non-null rows' — for instance when you need a percentage of a filtered subset, where you would keep SUM(CASE ...) on top and COUNT(*) underneath.

solutions.name: Window Function with AVG OVER
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT p.project_id,
       ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years) OVER (PARTITION BY p.project_id), 2) AS average_years
FROM Project p
JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id;
solutions.explanation: A window function computes the same per-project average but without collapsing the rows: PARTITION BY project_id defines the group, AVG is evaluated over each partition, and every detail row keeps the aggregate beside it. DISTINCT is then needed to fold the repeated rows back down, which makes this strictly more expensive than GROUP BY for this particular question — an extra sort or hash on top of the windowing pass. It earns its keep only when you also want the detail: keep the employee name and you can show each person next to their project's average, or subtract one from the other to see who is above or below the team norm. Use GROUP BY when you want one row per group, and a window when you want per-row context alongside the group figure.

edgeCases: Projects with no corresponding employees in the Employee table (returns NULL for experience years unless handled)
All employees in a project having NULL experience years (ROUND(AVG(...)) will result in NULL)

Percentage of Users Attended a Contest.title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
Percentage of Users Attended a Contest.problemStatement: Users holds one row per registered person on the site (user_id, user_name). Register holds one row per signup: a contest_id and the user_id of someone who registered for it, with (contest_id, user_id) as the primary key, so a user can register for a contest at most once. For every contest that appears in Register, report contest_id and percentage: what share of ALL users on the site registered for that contest, computed as registrations for the contest divided by the total number of rows in Users, times 100, rounded to two decimal places. The denominator is always the full user base, never the users of that contest. Sort the output by percentage from highest to lowest, and when two contests tie on percentage put the smaller contest_id first.

solutions.name: GROUP BY with a Scalar Subquery Denominator
solutions.query:
SELECT contest_id,
       ROUND(COUNT(user_id) * 100.0 / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users), 2) AS percentage
FROM Register
GROUP BY contest_id
ORDER BY percentage DESC, contest_id ASC;
solutions.explanation: The numerator varies per contest, the denominator does not, so the query groups Register by contest and divides by a constant that a scalar subquery computes once for the whole statement - the optimiser does not re-run it per group. Two details decide whether the arithmetic is right. Multiply by 100.0 rather than 100: with two integers MySQL and most engines would do integer division first and hand you 0 or 1, and writing one operand as a decimal forces floating-point maths. And ROUND(x, 2) must wrap the finished percentage, not the ratio. The primary key on (contest_id, user_id) is what lets COUNT(user_id) stand in for a distinct count; without it you would need COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) to avoid counting one person twice. Reach for this shape whenever a per-group number is being compared against one global total.

solutions.name: Total in a CTE, Attached with CROSS JOIN
solutions.query:
WITH total AS (
    SELECT COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM Users
)
SELECT r.contest_id,
       ROUND(COUNT(r.user_id) * 100.0 / t.user_count, 2) AS percentage
FROM Register r
CROSS JOIN total t
GROUP BY r.contest_id, t.user_count
ORDER BY percentage DESC, r.contest_id ASC;
solutions.explanation: Same maths, but the global total becomes a named one-row table that is joined in rather than an expression buried inside a formula. A CROSS JOIN against a single row does not duplicate anything - every Register row simply gains a user_count column - and because that column is now functionally part of each group it must be listed in GROUP BY, which is worth internalising about strict grouping rules. Choose this when the denominator grows into something you cannot inline: two or three global constants, a total that itself needs filtering, or a value you want to display alongside the percentage. It is also far easier to debug, since you can run the CTE on its own and see the number. The trade-off is verbosity - for one constant the scalar subquery says the same thing in one line.

solutions.name: Full Grid + Conditional Aggregation (CASE)
solutions.query:
SELECT c.contest_id,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN r.user_id IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS percentage
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT contest_id FROM Register) c
CROSS JOIN Users u
LEFT JOIN Register r
       ON r.contest_id = c.contest_id
      AND r.user_id = u.user_id
GROUP BY c.contest_id
ORDER BY percentage DESC, c.contest_id ASC;
solutions.explanation: A completely different mental model: build every contest-user pair that COULD have existed, mark each pair as registered or not, and let the percentage fall out as hits over opportunities. COUNT(*) per group is now exactly the number of users, so the denominator needs no separate query at all. The CASE inside SUM is the conditional aggregation idiom - it lets one pass answer several questions at once, which is why this shape wins the moment the report needs more columns, say the percentage of users who registered AND submitted. Note why the flag tests IS NOT NULL: after the LEFT JOIN, r.user_id is filled in only for the grid cells where a real registration matched, and is NULL for the cells where that user never signed up - so `r.user_id IS NOT NULL` literally means "this user did register for this contest". (The CASE itself never produces a NULL, thanks to its ELSE 0, so SUM's habit of skipping NULLs plays no part here.) COUNT(*) then counts every cell of the grid for that contest, which is exactly the whole user base - and that is why no separate denominator query is needed. The cost is real - you materialise users x contests rows - so keep it for reporting grids rather than huge tables.

edgeCases: Users registered in contests who are not present in the Users table (unlikely under FK constraints, but division would be off if so)
Some users registered in zero contests (they will not appear in the contest list, which is correct)

Queries Quality and Percentage.title: Queries Quality and Percentage
Queries Quality and Percentage.problemStatement: One table, Queries, where each row records a single result that a search engine returned for a named query: query_name identifies the search, result is the item shown, position is the rank at which it was shown (1 is the top slot), and rating is the score a user gave that result. There is no primary key, so the same query_name appears once per returned result. Report one row per query_name with two derived measures. The first, quality, is the average across that query's rows of rating divided by position, so a good result shown high scores well and a good result buried deep scores poorly. The second, poor_query_percentage, is the share of that query's rows whose rating is below 3, expressed as a percentage of that query's total row count. Both numbers are rounded to two decimal places. Rows may be returned in any order.

solutions.name: Conditional Aggregation (SUM of CASE)
solutions.query:
SELECT query_name,
       ROUND(AVG(rating * 1.0 / position), 2) AS quality,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN rating < 3 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2)
           AS poor_query_percentage
FROM Queries
WHERE query_name IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY query_name;
solutions.explanation: One pass, one grouping, two different summaries of the same bucket. AVG handles quality directly once the ratio is forced into floating point with the 1.0 factor, otherwise integer division would turn 2/5 into 0 and quietly report zero quality. The percentage uses the conditional aggregation idiom: CASE turns each row into 1 when it is poor and 0 otherwise, so SUM counts exactly the poor rows while COUNT(*) still counts them all, and the two live in the same aggregate without a second scan or a join. Multiplying by 100.0 rather than 100 keeps the division in floating point again. Reach for CASE inside an aggregate whenever you need counts of different subsets of the same group side by side; it is the tool that replaces several correlated subqueries with one traversal.

solutions.name: AVG of a 0/1 Indicator
solutions.query:
SELECT query_name,
       ROUND(AVG(rating * 1.0 / position), 2) AS quality,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN rating < 3 THEN 100.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2)
           AS poor_query_percentage
FROM Queries
WHERE query_name IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY query_name;
solutions.explanation: The insight is that a percentage is just an average of an indicator. Instead of counting the poor rows and dividing by the total, each row is mapped to 100 when it is poor and 0 when it is not, and AVG performs the division for you, since the mean of those numbers is by definition the percentage. That removes the explicit COUNT(*) denominator and with it a whole class of mistakes, most notably writing COUNT(rating) instead of COUNT(*) and having NULL ratings silently shrink the denominator. It is also the form that generalises: swap the constants for a value and you have a conditional average, or wrap it in a window and you have a running rate. The trade is that it hides the denominator, so a reader who wants to see the row count still has to add COUNT(*) back.

solutions.name: Correlated Subquery for the Poor Count
solutions.query:
SELECT q.query_name,
       ROUND(AVG(q.rating * 1.0 / q.position), 2) AS quality,
       ROUND((SELECT COUNT(*)
              FROM Queries p
              WHERE p.query_name = q.query_name
                AND p.rating < 3) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2)
           AS poor_query_percentage
FROM Queries q
WHERE q.query_name IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY q.query_name;
solutions.explanation: This keeps the grouped average but computes the poor-row count in a separate correlated pass keyed on the group's own name, which is legal because query_name is the grouping column and therefore has a single value per group. It is worth seeing because it shows the seam between the two measures explicitly, and because the same pattern is the only option when the extra count has to come from a different table entirely rather than from the rows being grouped. The cost is real: the subquery runs once per group and rescans Queries each time, whereas conditional aggregation gets the same number for free during the pass it was already making. Use it when the condition cannot be evaluated from the grouped rows themselves, and prefer CASE aggregation whenever it can.

edgeCases: query_name is NULL (the where filter ignores these)
Queries with high position numbers causing small ratios
0% or 100% poor queries for a query name

Monthly Transactions I.title: Monthly Transactions I
Monthly Transactions I.problemStatement: The Transactions table records card payments, one row per transaction: id is the primary key, country is the two-letter country the payment came from, state is either 'approved' or 'declined', amount is the value of the payment, and trans_date is the day it happened. Produce a monthly report per country. Bucket the rows by calendar month, formatted as 'YYYY-MM', and by country, and for every bucket that has at least one transaction return six columns: month, country, trans_count (how many transactions fell in the bucket), approved_count (how many of them had state 'approved'), trans_total_amount (the summed amount of all of them) and approved_total_amount (the summed amount of the approved ones only). A bucket with no approved transactions still appears, with zeros in the two approved columns. Rows may be returned in any order.
Monthly Transactions I.schema:
CREATE TABLE Transactions (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    country VARCHAR(4),
    state VARCHAR(10),
    amount INT,
    trans_date DATE
);

solutions.name: Conditional Aggregation (SUM of CASE)
solutions.query:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       country,
       COUNT(id) AS trans_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approved_count,
       SUM(amount) AS trans_total_amount,
       SUM(CASE WHEN state = 'approved' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS approved_total_amount
FROM Transactions
GROUP BY month, country;
solutions.explanation: One pass, one grouping, four aggregates. DATE_FORMAT collapses each date to its 'YYYY-MM' bucket and that expression, together with country, defines the group. The trick worth internalising is conditional aggregation: instead of filtering rows away in WHERE — which would also remove them from the unconditional totals — the CASE moves the filter inside the aggregate, contributing 1 or the amount for approved rows and 0 for the rest. That is how one scan can answer two different populations at once, and it is why the declined-only buckets still emit 0 rather than vanishing. The alternative of writing WHERE state = 'approved' anywhere in this query would be a bug. Cost is a single sort or hash on (month, country); this is the shape to reach for whenever a report needs 'total' and 'total where X' side by side.

solutions.name: Two Grouped Subqueries Joined (LEFT JOIN)
solutions.query:
SELECT t.month,
       t.country,
       t.trans_count,
       IFNULL(a.approved_count, 0) AS approved_count,
       t.trans_total_amount,
       IFNULL(a.approved_total_amount, 0) AS approved_total_amount
FROM (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, country,
           COUNT(*) AS trans_count, SUM(amount) AS trans_total_amount
    FROM Transactions
    GROUP BY month, country
) t
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT DATE_FORMAT(trans_date, '%Y-%m') AS month, country,
           COUNT(*) AS approved_count, SUM(amount) AS approved_total_amount
    FROM Transactions
    WHERE state = 'approved'
    GROUP BY month, country
) a ON a.month = t.month AND a.country = t.country;
solutions.explanation: The opposite mental model: build two independent reports and stitch them together. The left subquery aggregates everything, the right one aggregates only approved rows using an ordinary WHERE, and the join reunites them on the bucket key. The join must be a LEFT JOIN, because a month/country with no approvals has no row on the right at all; an INNER JOIN would delete that bucket from the report, which is the single most common bug in this shape. IFNULL then converts the padded NULLs into the 0 the report wants — NULL and 0 mean quite different things here, and only 0 is correct. The cost is two scans and two aggregations plus a join instead of one pass, so on a large table this is measurably slower than conditional aggregation. Reach for it when the two populations come from genuinely different tables or need different grain, and prefer the CASE version whenever both come from the same scan.

edgeCases: No approved transactions in a month/country group (the count and amount must evaluate to 0 instead of NULL)
country is NULL (grouping handles NULL values properly)

Immediate Food Delivery II.title: Immediate Food Delivery II
Immediate Food Delivery II.problemStatement: The Delivery table records one row per food order: delivery_id identifies the order, customer_id says who placed it, order_date is the day it was placed, and customer_pref_delivery_date is the day the customer asked to receive it. An order is called immediate when those two dates are identical and scheduled when the preferred date is later. Each customer's first order is the one carrying their earliest order_date, and if a customer placed more than one order on that earliest day then each of those rows counts as a first order for this tally. Return a single row with a single column named immediate_percentage: the share of all those first orders that were immediate, expressed as a percentage of the number of first orders and rounded to two decimal places.

solutions.name: Correlated Subquery for Each Customer's Earliest Date
solutions.query:
SELECT ROUND(
           SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS immediate_percentage
FROM Delivery d
WHERE d.order_date = (
    SELECT MIN(d2.order_date)
    FROM Delivery d2
    WHERE d2.customer_id = d.customer_id
);
solutions.explanation: The problem is really two problems stacked: pick the right rows, then measure them. This version picks rows the way a human would, asking of each order 'is this the earliest date my customer ever ordered on?'
