The correlated subquery computes that customer's MIN(order_date) and the WHERE keeps only matching rows; note that it keeps every row tied on that earliest date, which is why customer 4 contributes two rows here. Count them: five rows survive (delivery_id 1, 2, 5, 7 and 8) and three of those are immediate (2, 7 and 8), so the answer is 3/5 = 60.00. The measurement is conditional aggregation: the CASE turns each surviving row into 1 for immediate or 0 for scheduled, SUM adds up the immediate ones, COUNT(*) gives the denominator, and the 100.0 forces floating point so integer division cannot silently produce 0. Cost is one grouped lookup per outer row unless the optimiser rewrites it. Reach for this first when you are learning the pattern, because the WHERE clause reads like the English sentence in the question.

solutions.name: Join to a Derived Table of First Order Dates
solutions.query:
SELECT ROUND(
           SUM(CASE WHEN d.order_date = d.customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS immediate_percentage
FROM Delivery d
JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_date
    FROM Delivery
    GROUP BY customer_id
) f
  ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id
 AND f.first_date = d.order_date;
solutions.explanation: Same two steps, opposite mechanics. Instead of asking the question once per row, this builds the answer table once: a GROUP BY produces one row per customer holding their earliest order date, and an inner join then keeps only the orders that match their customer's first date. It is set thinking rather than row thinking, and it is normally the faster of the two because the aggregate is computed in a single pass and the join can use a hash or an index rather than repeating a scan per row. The join is on the pair (customer_id, order_date), which matters: joining on customer_id alone would multiply every order by its customer's first order. Like the correlated version it keeps ties, so a customer with two orders on the earliest day contributes both. Reach for this shape whenever the per-group summary is useful in its own right or you want to select extra columns from it.

solutions.name: Row Constructor IN
solutions.query:
SELECT ROUND(
           SUM(CASE WHEN order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS immediate_percentage
FROM Delivery
WHERE (customer_id, order_date) IN (
    SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date)
    FROM Delivery
    GROUP BY customer_id
);
solutions.explanation: This is the join written as a membership test. MySQL lets you compare a tuple, so (customer_id, order_date) IN (...) asks whether the pair appears in the list of (customer, earliest date) pairs produced by the GROUP BY. It is compact and it expresses the intent, 'this row is one of the first orders', in a single predicate with no alias juggling. Two warnings. First, row-constructor IN is not portable to every engine and older MySQL versions optimised it poorly, materialising the subquery and testing row by row. Second, IN inherits the usual NULL hazard: it is safe here because both columns are populated, but the negated form, NOT IN, returns no rows at all if the subquery ever produces a NULL in either position, so an anti-join or NOT EXISTS is the safer reflex for exclusion. Reach for this when the matching key is a natural pair and you only need to filter, not to read columns from the other side.

solutions.name: RANK Window Function
solutions.query:
SELECT ROUND(
           SUM(CASE WHEN order_date = customer_pref_delivery_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
           * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS immediate_percentage
FROM (
    SELECT order_date,
           customer_pref_delivery_date,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS rk
    FROM Delivery
) t
WHERE rk = 1;
solutions.explanation: Rather than computing a minimum and matching back to it, this ranks each customer's orders by date and keeps the winners. PARTITION BY customer_id restarts the numbering for every customer and ORDER BY order_date puts the earliest first, so rk = 1 marks the first order. The choice of ranking function is the whole lesson: RANK gives every row tied on the earliest date the value 1, matching the other three queries, whereas ROW_NUMBER would arbitrarily pick one of customer 4's two same-day orders and change the answer. Cost is a single sort of the table with no self-reference, often the cheapest plan, and the derived table can carry any other columns you need. Reach for window functions when the rule is 'top N per group' rather than a flat filter, because extending this to the two earliest orders is just rk <= 2 while the other shapes would need rewriting.

edgeCases: A customer with two orders on their earliest date - customer 4 in the sample data. Both rows count as first orders, which is exactly why the last solution uses RANK and not ROW_NUMBER.
All first orders are immediate (100.00%) or all are scheduled (0.00%)

Game Play Analysis IV.title: Game Play Analysis IV
Game Play Analysis IV.problemStatement: The Activity table logs one row per player per day of play, keyed on (player_id, event_date), recording the device used and how many games were played that day. A day with no row means the player did not log in that day. The task is to measure day-one retention: consider each player's very first login date, which is the minimum event_date for that player, and ask whether that same player also has a row on the calendar day immediately after it. Report a single column, fraction, equal to the number of players who did log in on that next day divided by the total number of distinct players in the table, rounded to 2 decimal places. Later consecutive-day pairs do not count - only the day right after the first login - and a player is counted at most once no matter how much they played.
Game Play Analysis IV.schema:
CREATE TABLE Activity (
    player_id INT,
    device_id INT,
    event_date DATE,
    games_played INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (player_id, event_date)
);

solutions.name: CTE of First Logins Joined to the Next Day
solutions.query:
WITH FirstLogin AS (
    SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date
    FROM Activity
    GROUP BY player_id
)
SELECT 
    ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT a.player_id) * 1.0 / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT player_id) FROM Activity), 2) AS fraction
FROM FirstLogin f
JOIN Activity a ON f.player_id = a.player_id 
    AND a.event_date = DATE_ADD(f.first_date, INTERVAL 1 DAY);
solutions.explanation: The CTE reduces the log to one row per player carrying their first login date, and the inner join then asks the retention question directly: does an Activity row exist for that player on first_date plus one day? Because the join is inner, only retained players survive, so COUNT(DISTINCT a.player_id) is the numerator; the denominator has to be a separate scalar subquery over the untouched Activity table, since the unretained players are no longer present in the join output. Multiplying by 1.0 forces the division into floating point - integer division would floor the answer to 0 in strict engines. Reach for this shape first: two clearly named steps, each one testable on its own. The one thing to watch is that DATE_ADD with INTERVAL is MySQL syntax; other engines spell the same idea as first_date + 1 or DATEADD, so the logic is portable even though the token is not.

solutions.name: EXISTS Test Per Player
solutions.query:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM Activity b
           WHERE b.player_id = f.player_id
             AND DATEDIFF(b.event_date, f.first_date) = 1
       ) THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END), 2) AS fraction
FROM (SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_date
      FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id) f;
solutions.explanation: This reframes the problem as one yes/no question per player rather than as a join that filters players away. The derived table gives exactly one row per player, EXISTS answers whether the day-after row is there, and CASE turns that boolean into 1.0 or 0.0 - at which point AVG is literally the fraction being asked for, with no separate denominator subquery to keep in sync. That is the real advantage: the numerator and denominator can never drift apart, because every player contributes exactly one term. EXISTS also stops at the first matching row instead of gathering all of them, so it never needs the DISTINCT that a join demands to avoid double counting a player. The cost is a correlated lookup per player, fine with the (player_id, event_date) primary key and slower without it. Reach for this whenever the answer is a rate over a fixed population.

solutions.name: Window Function MIN OVER
solutions.query:
WITH t AS (
    SELECT player_id, event_date,
           MIN(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS first_date
    FROM Activity
)
SELECT ROUND(
         COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(event_date, first_date) = 1 THEN player_id END) * 1.0
         / COUNT(DISTINCT player_id), 2) AS fraction
FROM t;
solutions.explanation: A window function computes each player's first login without collapsing the rows, so every original row keeps both its own event_date and its player's first_date side by side. That means the whole answer can be built from one pass over the enriched row set: the conditional COUNT DISTINCT counts a player only when one of their rows sits exactly one day after their first, and the plain COUNT DISTINCT over the same rows gives the total player population - numerator and denominator from a single scan, no join and no correlated lookup. This is the shape to reach for when you need per-row context alongside per-group facts, or when the same partitioned value feeds several different measures. The CASE without an ELSE deliberately yields NULL for non-matching rows, and COUNT ignores NULLs, which is exactly how the filter gets expressed inside an aggregate.

edgeCases: A player logged in consecutively on other days but not on the day after their first login
Total number of players is 1

Number of Unique Subjects Taught by Each.title: Number of Unique Subjects Taught by Each Teacher
Number of Unique Subjects Taught by Each.problemStatement: The Teacher table records teaching assignments in a university. Each row says that a given teacher_id teaches a given subject_id inside a given dept_id. The same teacher can teach the same subject in more than one department, which produces several rows that are identical except for dept_id, so the raw row count for a teacher overstates how many subjects they actually cover. For every teacher that appears in the table, return their teacher_id together with a column named cnt holding the number of distinct subjects they teach, counting a subject once even when it shows up under several departments. Teachers absent from the table produce no row, and the result may be returned in any order.

solutions.name: GROUP BY with COUNT(DISTINCT)
solutions.query:
SELECT teacher_id,
       COUNT(DISTINCT subject_id) AS cnt
FROM Teacher
GROUP BY teacher_id;
solutions.explanation: One bucket per teacher, and inside each bucket the DISTINCT modifier de-duplicates subject_id before counting, so the same subject taught in two departments contributes one. Dropping DISTINCT is the single most common mistake on this question: plain COUNT(subject_id) counts rows, which would report three subjects for a teacher who teaches two, one of them in two departments. COUNT with DISTINCT also ignores NULL subject ids, which is usually what you want. The cost is a hash or sort per group to hold the distinct values, slightly more than a bare COUNT, but this is the shortest and clearest statement of the requirement and should be the default.

solutions.name: De-duplicate First in a Derived Table
solutions.explanation: This separates the two ideas the previous query fuses. The inner query throws away the department column and de-duplicates, producing exactly one row per teacher-subject pair; the outer query then only has to count rows, so a plain COUNT(*) is correct. Splitting it this way is worth doing when several distinct counts are needed at once, because COUNT(DISTINCT a), COUNT(DISTINCT b) in one pass can be expensive while a pre-flattened set is cheap to aggregate repeatedly. It is also easier to debug: run the inner SELECT alone and you can see the deduplicated pairs. The trade-off is materialising an intermediate result, and on a table with an index on (teacher_id, subject_id) the direct COUNT(DISTINCT) will usually win.

solutions.name: Correlated Scalar Subquery
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT t.teacher_id, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT s.subject_id) FROM Teacher s WHERE s.teacher_id = t.teacher_id) AS cnt
FROM Teacher t;
solutions.explanation: Here the outer query supplies the list of teachers and the subquery answers 'how many distinct subjects does this one teach' once per teacher. It reads almost like the English sentence, which is why beginners often land on it, but it is the most expensive of the three: without an index on teacher_id the subquery re-scans the table for every outer row, and the outer DISTINCT adds another de-duplication pass because the driving table still has one row per assignment. Reach for a correlated subquery when the per-row question genuinely cannot be folded into the same GROUP BY — different filters, a different table, or a count that ranges over rows the outer grouping has already discarded — and use GROUP BY whenever both live in the same scan.

edgeCases: A teacher teaches the same subject across different departments (distinct ensures it is counted only once)

User Activity for the Past 30 Days I.title: User Activity for the Past 30 Days I
User Activity for the Past 30 Days I.problemStatement: The Activity table logs interactions with the site. Each row is one action: user_id, session_id, activity_date and activity_type (open_session, end_session, scroll_down or send_message). One user can log many actions on the same day and across several sessions, so the table contains duplicate user/date combinations. Report the daily active user count over a 30-day window that ENDS on 2019-07-27 inclusive - that is every date from 2019-06-28 through 2019-07-27. A user counts as active on a day if they logged at least one action of any type that day, no matter how many they logged. Output two columns, day and active_users, with one row per date in the window that actually has activity; days with no activity are left out entirely rather than reported as zero, and the rows may come back in any order.

solutions.name: Filter the Window, then COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)
solutions.query:
SELECT activity_date AS day,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
FROM Activity
WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27'
GROUP BY activity_date;
solutions.explanation: Filter first, then group - the two-step that answers most 'per day' questions. The window is written out as two literal endpoints, and the arithmetic that beginners get wrong is the inclusive count: a 30-day window ending 2019-07-27 starts on 2019-06-28, not 2019-06-27, because both ends are counted. DISTINCT inside COUNT is the whole reason this query is correct - the log holds several actions per user per day, and COUNT(*) would report actions, not people. Because the filter sits in WHERE rather than HAVING, the engine can use an index on activity_date and discard rows before any grouping work happens, which is the cheaper order. Days with no rows simply never form a group, matching the requirement to omit them; producing zeros would need a calendar table to LEFT JOIN against.

solutions.name: Deduplicate First, then Plain COUNT(*)
solutions.query:
SELECT day,
       COUNT(*) AS active_users
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT activity_date AS day, user_id
    FROM Activity
    WHERE activity_date BETWEEN '2019-06-28' AND '2019-07-27'
) AS daily_users
GROUP BY day;
solutions.explanation: Split the problem in two: the inner query reduces the log to the set of distinct (day, user) facts - 'this person was here that day' - and the outer query just counts the facts per day. It returns the same numbers as COUNT(DISTINCT ...) but makes the reasoning explicit, and that pays off in two situations. First, when you need several distinct counts in one query, engines that struggle with multiple COUNT(DISTINCT) expressions handle the pre-deduplicated version much better. Second, the inner result is exactly the table you would reuse to answer follow-ups such as average active days per user. The cost is materialising the intermediate set, and the trap to avoid is putting the date filter only on the outer query - filter inside so the DISTINCT works over the smaller set.

solutions.name: Anchor the Window with DATEDIFF
solutions.query:
SELECT activity_date AS day,
       COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
FROM Activity
WHERE DATEDIFF('2019-07-27', activity_date) BETWEEN 0 AND 29
GROUP BY activity_date;
solutions.explanation: Instead of naming both endpoints, this expresses the window as a distance from the single date the question actually gives you: how many days before 2019-07-27 did this happen? Zero through twenty-nine is thirty days inclusive, and writing it that way removes the off-by-one argument about whether the range starts on the 27th or 28th. The lower bound of 0 matters as much as the upper one - drop it and future-dated rows would leak in with negative differences. In MySQL you can spell the same idea as activity_date > DATE_SUB('2019-07-27', INTERVAL 30 DAY) AND activity_date <= '2019-07-27'. The catch, and the reason the literal BETWEEN version is usually preferred in production, is that wrapping the column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable: the engine can no longer seek an index on activity_date and must evaluate every row.

edgeCases: Dates outside the 30-day window (must be filtered out)
Users performing multiple activities on the same day (must be counted only once)

Product Sales Analysis III.title: Product Sales Analysis III
Product Sales Analysis III.problemStatement: Sales holds one row per sale with sale_id, product_id, year, quantity and price; the triple (sale_id, product_id, year) identifies a row, and Product maps each product_id to a product_name. For every product that was sold at least once, find the earliest year in which it sold anything and report that product_id, that year under the name first_year, and the quantity and price recorded on the sale from that year. The comparison is per product: each product gets its own earliest year, and later years for the same product are discarded even if they sold more. If a product happens to have several sales rows in its own first year, every one of those rows is reported, because the question fixes the year rather than picking a single sale. Products that were never sold produce no rows. Any output order is acceptable.

solutions.name: Join to Each Product's Earliest Year
solutions.query:
SELECT s.product_id,
       s.year AS first_year,
       s.quantity,
       s.price
FROM Sales s
JOIN (
    SELECT product_id, MIN(year) AS first_year
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY product_id
) f
  ON f.product_id = s.product_id
 AND f.first_year = s.year;
solutions.explanation: This is the standard cure for the beginner instinct of writing MIN(year) beside quantity and price in one grouped select, which is either rejected or, worse, silently returns the minimum year next to some unrelated row's quantity. The fix is to compute the summary alone in a derived table, one row per product, then join it back to the detail rows so the quantity and price come from the very rows that carry the winning year. Because it is a join, a product with two sales in its first year contributes both rows rather than one. It costs two passes over Sales plus a join, and it is the shape to reach for whenever the phrase 'the row where some column is smallest or largest' appears, since the summary and the detail stay cleanly separated.

solutions.name: Row-Value IN Against MIN(year)
solutions.query:
SELECT product_id,
       year AS first_year,
       quantity,
       price
FROM Sales
WHERE (product_id, year) IN (
    SELECT product_id, MIN(year)
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY product_id
);
solutions.explanation: Same two-pass idea, written as a set membership test on a pair of columns instead of a join, which avoids inventing an alias for the derived table and keeps the select list free of table prefixes. The pairing is the whole point: testing year IN (SELECT MIN(year) ...) without the product_id would be a real bug, because it would let a product through whenever its year matched some other product's first year. MySQL and SQLite both support these row constructors, though not every engine does. Also remember the asymmetry with NULLs: IN just fails to match a NULL, but the negated NOT IN over a subquery containing one NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row and returns nothing at all. Pick this form for readability when no extra summary columns are needed.

solutions.name: NOT EXISTS (No Earlier Sale)
solutions.query:
SELECT s.product_id,
       s.year AS first_year,
       s.quantity,
       s.price
FROM Sales s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Sales e
    WHERE e.product_id = s.product_id
      AND e.year < s.year
);
solutions.explanation: This one never computes a minimum at all. It redefines 'earliest' as 'nothing earlier exists', so each sale is kept only when no other sale of the same product carries a smaller year. The anti-join reading is often the fastest in practice because EXISTS can stop at the first offending row instead of aggregating the whole partition, and an index on (product_id, year) turns each probe into a single seek. It is also the NULL-safe counterpart to NOT IN: NOT EXISTS is driven by row existence rather than by three-valued comparison, so a stray NULL cannot wipe out the result set the way it would with NOT IN. Reach for it when the requirement is naturally phrased as an absence, such as 'customers who never ordered' or 'the first event per key'.

solutions.name: Window Function (RANK by Year)
solutions.query:
SELECT product_id, first_year, quantity, price
FROM (
    SELECT product_id,
           year AS first_year,
           quantity,
           price,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY year ASC) AS rnk
    FROM Sales
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
solutions.explanation: The window form makes one pass, sorting each product's sales by year and labelling them, after which the answer is simply the rows labelled 1. It carries quantity and price along for free, which is exactly what the grouped-aggregate attempt could not do. RANK rather than ROW_NUMBER is deliberate: if a product had two sales in the same earliest year, ROW_NUMBER would keep only one of them arbitrarily and diverge from the other three solutions, whereas RANK ties them both at 1. The window filter has to live in an outer query or a CTE because the alias rnk does not exist yet in the WHERE clause of its own select. Choose this when the requirement may grow into the first two years, or a comparison against the following sale via LAG.

edgeCases: Products with multiple transactions in their first year (this query correctly returns all of them)
Products that have never been sold (they will not appear in the Sales table, so they won't be returned)

Classes More Than 5 Students.title: Classes More Than 5 Students
Classes More Than 5 Students.problemStatement: The Courses table records enrolments, one row per student per class, with (student, class) as the primary key. Because that pair is unique, a student can never be listed twice in the same class, so counting rows in a class is the same as counting distinct students in it; a student may of course appear in several different classes. Report the name of every class that has at least five students enrolled — five counts, so the comparison is >= 5 and not > 5, which is the trap the title sets. Classes with four or fewer enrolments are excluded entirely rather than reported with a count. Return a single column named class, one row per qualifying class, in any order.

solutions.name: GROUP BY with HAVING
solutions.query:
SELECT class
FROM Courses
GROUP BY class
HAVING COUNT(student) >= 5;
solutions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses the enrolment rows into one row per class, and HAVING filters those groups after the counting has happened. The distinction between WHERE and HAVING is the whole lesson: WHERE runs before grouping and can only see individual rows, so COUNT is not available to it, while HAVING runs after and sees the aggregate. Because (student, class) is the primary key, COUNT(student) and COUNT(*) agree here; if duplicates were possible you would need COUNT(DISTINCT student) to avoid inflating a class with a repeated student. Note also that COUNT(student) ignores NULL students whereas COUNT(*) would not, which is a meaningful difference on a nullable column. This is the canonical answer: one grouping pass, no self-reference, and it is what an interviewer expects to see first.

solutions.name: Correlated Subquery Counting Siblings
solutions.explanation: Here the query never groups. It walks the enrolment rows one at a time and, for each, asks a correlated subquery how many rows share that class; if the answer is at least five the class name survives. DISTINCT is mandatory, because every one of Math's rows independently passes the test and would otherwise be emitted, giving five copies of 'Math' — forgetting it is the characteristic bug of this shape. The cost is real: the subquery is logically evaluated once per row rather than once per class, so the work is roughly rows x rows without an index on class, against a single pass for GROUP BY. It is worth understanding because the same pattern is the only way to express some per-row conditions, but for a plain 'groups above a threshold' question HAVING is strictly better.

solutions.name: Window Function COUNT OVER (PARTITION BY)
solutions.explanation: A window function computes the class size without collapsing the rows: PARTITION BY class defines the peer group, COUNT(*) OVER that partition stamps every enrolment row with how many rows its class has, and the outer query then filters on that stamp. Because the rows survive the aggregate, DISTINCT is needed to fold Math's five stamped rows back into one output row. The window value cannot be referenced in the same query's WHERE clause — window functions are evaluated after WHERE — which is exactly why the derived table (or a CTE) is required; that ordering rule is the thing to remember. Cost is one sort or hash by class, comparable to GROUP BY. Reach for this shape when you need the per-group number alongside the individual rows, for example to list each student together with their class size; when you only want the qualifying class names, GROUP BY plus HAVING says it with less machinery.

edgeCases: Classes with exactly 5 students (should be included)
No classes matching the filter (returns empty result set)

Find Followers Count.title: Find Followers Count
Find Followers Count.problemStatement: The Followers table stores edges of a social graph: each row says that the person identified by follower_id follows the person identified by user_id. The pair (user_id, follower_id) is the primary key, so the same follower can never be recorded twice for the same user and every row is a distinct relationship. For each user who appears in the user_id column, return that user_id together with followers_count, the number of people who follow them. Somebody who only ever shows up as a follower_id and is never followed by anyone has no rows of their own here and therefore does not appear in the output at all, rather than appearing with a count of zero. The result is ordered by user_id in ascending order.

solutions.name: GROUP BY with COUNT
solutions.query:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(follower_id) AS followers_count
FROM Followers
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id ASC;
solutions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses all rows sharing a user_id into one output row, and COUNT then measures how many rows fell into each bucket, which is exactly the number of followers because every row is one follow relationship. COUNT(follower_id) counts non-NULL values of that column while COUNT(*) counts rows; they agree here only because follower_id is part of the primary key and can never be NULL, and knowing that difference is what keeps you out of trouble on nullable columns. The primary key also means duplicates are impossible, so COUNT(DISTINCT follower_id) would be honest but wasteful. Cost is one pass plus a grouping, and if an index leads on user_id the engine can stream the groups out already sorted, making the ORDER BY nearly free. This is the default tool: when the question says 'for each X, how many Y', reach for GROUP BY before anything else.

solutions.name: Window COUNT with DISTINCT
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS followers_count
FROM Followers
ORDER BY user_id ASC;
solutions.explanation: A window function computes the same count but does not collapse anything: PARTITION BY user_id defines the group, COUNT(*) OVER that partition stamps the group's size onto every row belonging to it, and DISTINCT is then needed to reduce the four stamped rows back to one per user. That extra deduplication step is precisely the cost of the approach, and it is why GROUP BY is the better choice for this exact question. The reason to know this shape is that it keeps the detail rows alive: if the task also wanted each follower listed next to the total, or the follower's share of the total, the aggregate version would have to join back to the table while the window version already has both numbers on the same row. Note also that a window function cannot appear in WHERE, so filtering on followers_count requires wrapping this in a derived table or CTE.

solutions.name: Correlated Subquery per User
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT f.user_id,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT f2.follower_id)
        FROM Followers f2
        WHERE f2.user_id = f.user_id) AS followers_count
FROM Followers f
ORDER BY f.user_id ASC;
solutions.explanation: This flips the direction of the work: instead of letting the engine bucket rows, it produces the list of users first and then asks a separate counting question about each one. The scalar subquery is correlated through f2.user_id = f.user_id, so it returns one number per outer row, and DISTINCT removes the repeats that come from scanning the base table for the user list. It is the most expensive of the three, potentially one aggregate lookup per row, and the DISTINCT is a second sort on top of that. It earns its place when the outer list comes from a different table, for example a Users table where you want every user including those with zero followers: a correlated COUNT returns 0 naturally there, while GROUP BY over Followers can never invent a row for someone with no followers and would need a LEFT JOIN to do the same job.

edgeCases: Users with 0 followers (they will not be present in the Followers table)

Biggest Single Number.title: Biggest Single Number
Biggest Single Number.problemStatement: MyNumbers is a single-column table of integers with no key and no uniqueness guarantee, so the same value may be listed several times. A value is called a single number when it occurs on exactly one row of the whole table; a value appearing twice or more is not single, no matter how many times. Return one column named num holding the largest single number in the table. The result must always be exactly one row: when the table contains no single number at all - because every value repeats, or because the table is empty - report NULL rather than returning zero rows. That NULL requirement is the part that shapes the query, since any approach that filters rows and then takes the top one would return an empty result set instead of a row containing NULL.

solutions.name: GROUP BY / HAVING, Then MAX
solutions.query:
SELECT MAX(num) AS num
FROM (
    SELECT num
    FROM MyNumbers
    GROUP BY num
    HAVING COUNT(num) = 1
) AS unique_nums;
solutions.explanation: The inner query collapses the table to one row per distinct value and HAVING keeps only the values whose group has size one, which is the definition of single. The outer MAX then picks the largest of what remains. Reaching for MAX rather than ORDER BY num DESC LIMIT 1 is the deliberate choice here: an aggregate with no GROUP BY always produces exactly one row, so when the inner set is empty MAX returns NULL and the required single-row NULL answer falls out for free, whereas LIMIT 1 over an empty set returns no rows at all and fails the specification. Cost is one grouping pass, typically a sort or hash on num, and this is the shape to default to whenever the rule is stated in terms of how many times something occurs - counting per group is what GROUP BY exists for.

solutions.name: Correlated Count Subquery
solutions.explanation: This keeps the original rows and asks a question about each one: how many rows in the table share my value? Only rows answering one survive the WHERE, and MAX over the survivors gives the answer, again returning NULL rather than no rows when nothing survives. The mental model is per-row interrogation instead of per-group summarisation, and it is the shape to learn when you want to keep other columns from the row that a GROUP BY would have forced you to aggregate away. The cost is that the subquery is evaluated per row, so without an index on num it is quadratic where the grouped version is linearithmic - on a big table prefer the grouped form. Note the deliberate use of COUNT(*) here: COUNT(num) would skip NULL values, and while a NULL num can never equal m.num anyway, keeping the star makes the intent unambiguous.

solutions.name: Window Function COUNT OVER
solutions.explanation: A window function attaches the group's size to every row without folding the rows together, so each row travels alongside a count of how many times its value appears. Filtering on that count in the outer query keeps only the singletons, and MAX finishes the job with the same NULL-on-empty guarantee as the other shapes. Compared with GROUP BY this costs one partitioning pass and no collapse, and it is the tool to reach for the moment you need both the row-level detail and the group-level statistic in the same result - for instance if the task also asked for the smallest, or for other columns of the singleton row. Note that the count has to be filtered in the outer query, because a window function is evaluated after WHERE runs and therefore cannot be referenced in the WHERE of the same SELECT.

edgeCases: The table is empty or all numbers appear at least twice (the subquery is empty, and the outer query returns a single row containing NULL)

Customers Who Bought All Products.title: Customers Who Bought All Products
Customers Who Bought All Products.problemStatement: Product is a catalogue with one row per product_key, and that key is unique. Customer is a purchase log where each row says that a customer_id bought the product identified by product_key; the same customer may appear many times, once per product bought, and the same customer-product pair can in principle be logged more than once. Report the customer_id of every customer whose purchases cover the entire catalogue, meaning that for each product_key present in Product there is at least one matching purchase row for that customer. Buying the same product repeatedly does not help, and a customer who bought something not in the catalogue is neither rewarded nor punished for it. Return one row per qualifying customer, in any order.

solutions.name: GROUP BY with HAVING against the Catalogue Size
solutions.query:
SELECT customer_id
FROM Customer
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product);
solutions.explanation: Counting is the pragmatic way to prove coverage: if a customer's number of distinct products equals the total number of products in the catalogue, and every product they bought is in the catalogue, then they must have bought all of them. DISTINCT is essential because a repeated purchase would otherwise inflate the count and let a customer qualify without full coverage. The uncorrelated scalar subquery runs once, not once per group, so this is a single pass over Customer plus a tiny constant. The assumption to keep in mind is that Customer never references a product_key missing from Product; if it can, add a join to Product before grouping, otherwise a customer with enough junk keys could reach the target count.

solutions.name: Relational Division with Double NOT EXISTS
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id
FROM Customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Product p
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Customer c2
        WHERE c2.customer_id = c.customer_id
          AND c2.product_key = p.product_key
    )
);
solutions.explanation: This is the textbook answer to 'for all' questions, and it says exactly what the requirement says: keep a customer when there does not exist a product that this customer did not buy. It needs no counting, so duplicate purchase rows and catalogue keys the customer never heard of cannot skew it, and it stays correct even if Customer references products outside the catalogue. NOT EXISTS is also NULL-safe: the equivalent written with NOT IN would collapse to an empty result the moment a NULL product_key appeared in the inner set, because NULL makes every comparison unknown rather than false. The cost is a nested anti-join that can be quadratic without indexes, so prefer the counting form on large logs and this form when correctness under messy data matters more.

solutions.name: CROSS JOIN Every Pair and Check for Gaps
solutions.query:
SELECT ca.customer_id
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM Customer) ca
CROSS JOIN Product p
LEFT JOIN Customer c
       ON c.customer_id = ca.customer_id
      AND c.product_key = p.product_key
GROUP BY ca.customer_id
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN c.customer_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) = 0;
solutions.explanation: The CROSS JOIN manufactures the complete grid of customer-by-product combinations that ought to exist, the LEFT JOIN marks which of those cells were actually purchased, and the HAVING keeps only the customers with zero unmatched cells. It makes the missing-purchase idea visible as data rather than hiding it in a count comparison, and the same skeleton generalises immediately: swap the HAVING for '<= 1' to find near-complete customers, or select the unmatched rows instead to report exactly which products each customer still needs. The price is the full grid, customers times products rows before aggregation, so it is the wrong tool on a large catalogue and the right one when you want a gap report rather than a yes-or-no answer.

edgeCases: Customers who bought the same product multiple times (handled by COUNT(DISTINCT ...))
Empty Product table

The Number of Employees Which Report to.title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
The Number of Employees Which Report to.problemStatement: The Employees table describes a company as a self-referencing hierarchy. Each row is one person: employee_id, name, age, and reports_to, which holds the employee_id of that person's direct manager, or NULL for someone who reports to nobody. A manager is simply an employee whose employee_id appears in some other row's reports_to. Report every manager who has at least one DIRECT report, with four columns: employee_id, name, reports_count - how many people list them as their manager - and average_age, the mean age of exactly those direct reports rounded to the nearest whole number. Only direct reports count, so a manager's reports' own reports are not included, and employees with nobody reporting to them must not appear at all. Order the result by employee_id ascending.

solutions.name: Self-Join with GROUP BY
solutions.query:
SELECT m.employee_id,
       m.name,
       COUNT(e.employee_id) AS reports_count,
       ROUND(AVG(e.age)) AS average_age
FROM Employees m
JOIN Employees e ON e.reports_to = m.employee_id
GROUP BY m.employee_id, m.name
ORDER BY m.employee_id;
solutions.explanation: One table is playing two roles, so you alias it twice: m is the manager side, e is the report side, and the join condition e.reports_to = m.employee_id is literally the sentence 'e reports to m'. The INNER join is doing quiet work - a manager with no reports produces no matching e row and disappears, which is exactly what the question wants, and rows whose reports_to is NULL never match anything because NULL = anything is never true. After the join, each manager owns one row per report, so GROUP BY collapses them and the aggregates describe the reports rather than the manager. Note that AVG ignores NULL ages and divides by the count of non-NULL values, which is normally what you want; ROUND with no second argument gives the nearest integer. This is the shape to reach for by default: one pass, one join, no per-row subquery.

solutions.name: Aggregate First in a CTE, then Join Back for Names
solutions.query:
WITH report_stats AS (
    SELECT reports_to AS manager_id,
           COUNT(*) AS reports_count,
           ROUND(AVG(age)) AS average_age
    FROM Employees
    WHERE reports_to IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY reports_to
)
SELECT m.employee_id,
       m.name,
       r.reports_count,
       r.average_age
FROM report_stats r
JOIN Employees m ON m.employee_id = r.manager_id
ORDER BY m.employee_id;
solutions.explanation: Answer the numeric question on its own terms first: grouping the table by reports_to already gives one row per manager with the count and the average, and the only thing missing is the manager's name, which a second join fetches afterwards. Splitting the work like this is easier to reason about than a self-join whose GROUP BY mixes manager columns with report aggregates - and it removes the 'which columns must I list in GROUP BY' question, because the outer query does not aggregate at all. The explicit WHERE reports_to IS NOT NULL is documentation more than logic here (those rows would never find a manager to join to anyway), but it shrinks the group set immediately. This pattern also scales best: the CTE reads the table once, and if the hierarchy table were huge you would still be joining a small aggregated result to it.

solutions.name: Correlated Subqueries with EXISTS
solutions.query:
SELECT m.employee_id
     , m.name
     , (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Employees e WHERE e.reports_to = m.employee_id) AS reports_count
     , (SELECT ROUND(AVG(e.age)) FROM Employees e WHERE e.reports_to = m.employee_id) AS average_age
FROM Employees m
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Employees e WHERE e.reports_to = m.employee_id)
ORDER BY m.employee_id;
solutions.explanation: This version keeps the row set and the measurements separate: the outer query decides WHO appears - anybody somebody reports to, tested with EXISTS - and each subquery answers one question about that person. EXISTS is the right membership test here because it stops at the first match and, unlike NOT IN, is immune to NULLs: had you written the inverse filter as reports_to NOT IN (SELECT ...) and the subquery contained a single NULL, the comparison would evaluate to UNKNOWN for every row and the query would return nothing at all. The price is that the two correlated subqueries run once per candidate manager, so without an index on reports_to this is the slowest of the three. Its virtue is composability - adding 'youngest report' is one more subquery, with no risk of disturbing the existing grouping.

edgeCases: Employees who do not have any reports (automatically filtered out due to the INNER JOIN)
Floating point rounding behavior for reports' average age

Primary Department for Each Employee.title: Primary Department for Each Employee
Primary Department for Each Employee.problemStatement: One table, Employee, keyed on the pair (employee_id, department_id), so a row means 'this person belongs to this department' and a person may have several rows. The third column, primary_flag, is 'Y' when that department is the person's primary one and 'N' otherwise. The data follows two rules: someone attached to several departments has exactly one row flagged 'Y', while someone attached to a single department is always flagged 'N' because they were never asked to choose. Report every employee exactly once, as employee_id together with the department_id of their primary department. For a multi-department employee that is the department carrying the 'Y'; for a single-department employee it is their only department, despite its 'N' flag. Every employee_id present in the table appears in the output once, and rows may be returned in any order.

solutions.name: UNION of the Two Cases
solutions.query:
SELECT employee_id, department_id
FROM Employee
WHERE primary_flag = 'Y'
UNION
SELECT employee_id, department_id
FROM Employee
GROUP BY employee_id
HAVING COUNT(department_id) = 1;
solutions.explanation: The statement describes two disjoint populations, so the query simply answers each one and stacks the answers. The first branch is a plain filter for the explicit choice; the second finds employees whose whole membership list is a single row and returns that row, which is safe here precisely because the group has exactly one department_id to hand back. UNION rather than UNION ALL also dedupes as a safety net, though the two branches cannot overlap under the stated rules. This is the most direct translation of the specification and the easiest to verify line by line. Its weakness is that Employee is read twice and the shape does not extend gracefully if a third rule ever appears.

solutions.name: Single Filter with a Correlated Count
solutions.query:
SELECT e.employee_id, e.department_id
FROM Employee e
WHERE e.primary_flag = 'Y'
   OR (SELECT COUNT(*)
       FROM Employee x
       WHERE x.employee_id = e.employee_id) = 1;
solutions.explanation: Rather than producing two result sets and gluing them together, this keeps one scan of Employee and expresses both rules as a single OR predicate: keep the row if it is flagged, or if this employee has only one row in the whole table. Collapsing the union into a WHERE clause means there is only one select list to maintain and no chance of the two branches drifting apart in column order, a classic UNION bug since UNION matches by position and not by name. The price is the correlated count, which is logically evaluated per row and wants an index on employee_id. Use this when the branches share almost all of their logic; use the UNION when they genuinely select different things.

solutions.name: Window COUNT Over the Employee Partition
solutions.query:
SELECT employee_id, department_id
FROM (
    SELECT employee_id,
           department_id,
           primary_flag,
           COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id) AS dept_count
    FROM Employee
) t
WHERE primary_flag = 'Y' OR dept_count = 1;
solutions.explanation: This computes the same 'how many departments does this person have' number as the correlated subquery, but as a window aggregate that is calculated for every row in one pass instead of being re-derived per row. Because a window function does not collapse rows, primary_flag stays available beside the count, so the two rules can be applied together in the outer WHERE. It typically beats the correlated version on large inputs, since one partitioned pass replaces many lookups, and it beats the UNION by touching the table once. The filter must sit outside the subquery because window functions are evaluated after WHERE. Reach for this whenever you need a per-group statistic without losing the individual rows it was computed from.

solutions.name: ROW_NUMBER Ordered by the Flag
solutions.query:
SELECT employee_id, department_id
FROM (
    SELECT employee_id,
           department_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY employee_id
               ORDER BY primary_flag DESC, department_id ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Employee
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
solutions.explanation: A different framing altogether: instead of testing two conditions, rank each employee's rows so that the winner is always first, then take the first. Sorting primary_flag descending puts 'Y' ahead of 'N' because Y sorts after N, so a flagged row always wins its partition, and an employee with a single unflagged row wins by default with nothing to beat. ROW_NUMBER rather than RANK guarantees exactly one row per employee even if the data ever broke its own rule and carried two 'Y' rows, with department_id as a deterministic tie-break. This 'pick one row per group by a priority order' pattern is worth internalising because it solves a huge family of problems, latest order per customer, best score per player, with only the ORDER BY changing.

edgeCases: An employee belongs to only one department, which has a primary_flag of 'N' (correctly selected by the second part of the UNION)
An employee belongs to multiple departments and has one department marked 'Y' (correctly selected by the first part of the UNION)

Triangle Judgement.title: Triangle Judgement
Triangle Judgement.problemStatement: The Triangle table stores candidate line-segment triples, one row per triple, with columns x, y and z holding the three lengths and forming the primary key. Judge each row on its own and report whether those three lengths could be assembled into an actual triangle. The rule is the triangle inequality applied in all three directions: the triple is valid only when x + y > z and x + z > y and y + z > x, all strictly greater, so a degenerate case such as 1, 2, 3 where one sum merely equals the third side does not qualify. Return every input row unchanged — x, y and z — plus a fourth column named triangle holding the string 'Yes' when all three inequalities hold and 'No' otherwise. No rows are filtered out and no ordering is required.

solutions.name: CASE Expression with Three Inequalities
solutions.query:
SELECT x, y, z,
       CASE
           WHEN x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x THEN 'Yes'
           ELSE 'No'
       END AS triangle
FROM Triangle;
solutions.explanation: The requirement is a per-row computation, not a filter, so it belongs in the SELECT list rather than in WHERE — that is the key idea here. A CASE expression is SQL's if/else, producing one value per row, and because no rows are removed the output has exactly as many rows as the input. The three conditions are ANDed because the triangle inequality must hold for every pairing; ORing them would call 13, 15, 30 a triangle since 13 + 30 > 15. The comparisons are strict, which correctly rejects degenerate collinear triples where a sum equals the remaining side. ELSE is what keeps the 'No' rows from becoming NULL — a CASE with no ELSE returns NULL when nothing matches, and NULL is not the answer the report wants. Cost is a single scan with trivial arithmetic, and this is the version to write by default.

solutions.name: Compare the Perimeter Against the Longest Side
solutions.query:
SELECT x, y, z,
       CASE
           WHEN x + y + z > 2 * (CASE WHEN x >= y AND x >= z THEN x
                                      WHEN y >= z THEN y
                                      ELSE z END)
           THEN 'Yes'
           ELSE 'No'
       END AS triangle
FROM Triangle;
solutions.explanation: Three inequalities are really one in disguise: only the longest side can ever break the rule, since the other two sums already include it. So the whole test reduces to longest < sum of the other two, which rearranges to perimeter > 2 * longest. The inner CASE picks the maximum of the three columns by hand; in MySQL you can write GREATEST(x, y, z) instead and the query becomes a one-liner, but the expanded form makes the comparison chain explicit and stays portable. Cost is identical to the three-condition version — a single scan — so choose it not for speed but for what it teaches: when several predicates overlap, finding the one that dominates the others often collapses the logic. It also generalises well; with n segments the same reasoning gives a single check against the largest element rather than n separate ones.

solutions.name: UNION ALL of Two Complementary Filters
solutions.query:
SELECT x, y, z, 'Yes' AS triangle
FROM Triangle
WHERE x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x
UNION ALL
SELECT x, y, z, 'No' AS triangle
FROM Triangle
WHERE NOT (x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x);
solutions.explanation: Instead of labelling rows one by one, this partitions the table into two sets and tags each with a literal. It is the set-oriented way to think, and it is genuinely useful when the two branches need different joins or different columns rather than just a different label. The correctness condition is that the branches be exact complements: the second predicate is the literal negation of the first, so no row is emitted twice and none is lost. UNION ALL, not UNION, is the right operator here because the branches are disjoint by construction and UNION would pay for a needless de-duplication pass over the whole result. Costs two scans against the CASE version's one, and it would break if x, y or z were nullable, since NOT (UNKNOWN) is still UNKNOWN and such rows would fall through both branches and disappear. Prefer CASE for simple labelling; reach for UNION ALL when the branches diverge structurally.

edgeCases: A side length is 0 or negative: In real geometry, sides must be positive. The mathematical conditions x + y > z, etc., will naturally handle positive non-zero checks unless negative values cancel each other.
Degenerate triangle where the sum of two sides equals the third (e.g., 10, 10, 20): This does not form a valid triangle and will correctly return 'No' since the inequality is strictly greater than.

Consecutive Numbers.title: Consecutive Numbers
Consecutive Numbers.problemStatement: The Logs table has one row per log entry: id gives the entries their order and num is the value recorded at that point. The ids run consecutively with no gaps, so ordering by id reproduces the order in which the log was written. Report every distinct value of num that appears in at least three rows sitting directly next to each other in id order, that is, three back to back occurrences with nothing else in between. A value that occurs many times overall but never three times in an unbroken run does not qualify, a run longer than three still qualifies, and a value with several qualifying runs is still reported only once. The single output column is named ConsecutiveNums and the rows may be returned in any order.

solutions.name: Self-Join on ID Arithmetic
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT l1.num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM Logs l1
JOIN Logs l2 ON l2.id = l1.id + 1
JOIN Logs l3 ON l3.id = l1.id + 2
WHERE l1.num = l2.num AND l2.num = l3.num;
solutions.explanation: Three consecutive rows are wanted, so the table is brought in three times and glued together by id arithmetic: l2 is the row one id later and l3 the row two ids later. Once those three rows sit on a single output row the condition is a plain equality test, and DISTINCT collapses overlapping windows so a run of five identical values reports its number once instead of three times. The assumption this rests on is that ids are gapless and increasing; if a deleted row leaves a hole, l1.id + 1 matches nothing and a genuine run of three adjacent entries is missed, which is the single biggest reason to prefer the window versions in real data. Cost is two joins, cheap with an index on id but awkward to extend, since 'at least five in a row' means writing four joins. Reach for it when you have a trustworthy dense key and want an answer that any SQL dialect, however old, will run.

solutions.name: Window Functions (LAG)
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           LAG(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num,
           LAG(num, 2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_prev_num
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev_num AND num = prev_prev_num;
solutions.explanation: Rather than matching on id values, this uses position: ordering by id, LAG(num, 1) and LAG(num, 2) drag the two preceding rows' values onto the current row, so the three way comparison becomes three columns of one row. Because it works on row positions in the ordered sequence, it survives gaps in the id column that would break the self-join, which is usually the deciding argument. On the first two rows LAG returns NULL and the equality tests evaluate to UNKNOWN, so those rows drop out with no special handling, exactly as intended. DISTINCT is still required because every window of a long run produces a hit. Cost is a single ordered pass rather than two joins, and it is the more scalable plan. Reach for LAG whenever the rule mentions 'the previous row' or a small fixed lookback.

solutions.name: Gaps and Islands with ROW_NUMBER
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY num ORDER BY id) AS grp
    FROM Logs
) t
GROUP BY num, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
solutions.explanation: This is the general pattern for runs, and it is worth learning even though it looks like a magic trick. Numbering each value's own occurrences with ROW_NUMBER and subtracting that counter from the id produces a difference that stays constant exactly while the occurrences are adjacent and jumps whenever the run is interrupted, so (num, grp) is a unique label for one island. Grouping by that label and applying HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 then answers the question directly, and DISTINCT merges a value that has more than one qualifying island. The decisive advantage over LAG is that the threshold is data, not structure: asking for runs of ten is a change of one digit, whereas LAG needs nine extra columns and the self-join needs nine extra joins. It also hands you the run's length and boundaries if you want MIN(id) and MAX(id). Cost is one sort per partition plus a grouping.

edgeCases: Gaps in ID sequence: If IDs have gaps (e.g. 1, 2, 4), the self-join method on ID math may fail to find consecutive numbers, whereas the window function method will still work correctly because it uses positional order.
A number appears more than three times consecutively: The use of DISTINCT ensures that the number is returned exactly once.
Table contains fewer than three rows: Both queries will safely return an empty result set without failing.

Product Price at a Given Date.title: Product Price at a Given Date
Product Price at a Given Date.problemStatement: The Products table is a price-change log rather than a price list. Each row, keyed on (product_id, change_date), says that on change_date the product's price became new_price and stayed there until the next change for that product. Every product mentioned anywhere in the table implicitly started life at a default price of 10 before its first recorded change. Report product_id and price for every distinct product in the table, where price is the value in force on 2019-08-16: the new_price of that product's most recent change dated on or before 2019-08-16, or 10 when the product has no change on or before that date because all of its changes happen later. A change dated exactly 2019-08-16 counts as already applied. Each product appears once and rows may be returned in any order.

solutions.name: Latest Change per Product, UNION the Untouched Ones
solutions.query:
SELECT product_id, new_price AS price
FROM Products
WHERE (product_id, change_date) IN (
    SELECT product_id, MAX(change_date)
    FROM Products
    WHERE change_date <= '2019-08-16'
    GROUP BY product_id
)
UNION
SELECT DISTINCT product_id, 10 AS price
FROM Products
WHERE product_id NOT IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT product_id
    FROM Products
    WHERE change_date <= '2019-08-16'
);
solutions.explanation: The population splits cleanly in two, so the query does too. The first branch finds, per product, the latest change date on or before the cut-off and then matches the row-value pair (product_id, change_date) back against the log to recover that row's price - matching the pair rather than the date alone is what stops one product borrowing another's change date. The second branch handles products whose entire history lies after the cut-off and hands them the default 10. Because the two branches are disjoint by construction, UNION ALL would be equally correct and slightly cheaper. The trap worth memorising is in the NOT IN: if that inner subquery could ever produce a NULL product_id, every comparison becomes UNKNOWN and the whole branch returns zero rows silently - here product_id is part of the primary key so it cannot be NULL, but NOT EXISTS is the habit to build.

solutions.name: All Products LEFT JOINed to Their Latest Change
solutions.query:
SELECT DISTINCT p1.product_id, COALESCE(p2.new_price, 10) AS price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products) p1
LEFT JOIN Products p2 ON p1.product_id = p2.product_id
  AND p2.change_date = (
      SELECT MAX(change_date)
      FROM Products p3
      WHERE p3.product_id = p1.product_id AND p3.change_date <= '2019-08-16'
  );
solutions.explanation: Rather than splitting the products into two sets and gluing the results back together, this drives from the complete list of products once and lets an outer join decide what each one gets. The correlated MAX inside the ON clause names the relevant change row, and when a product has no change on or before the cut-off that subquery returns NULL, nothing matches, the LEFT JOIN preserves the product with NULL columns, and COALESCE substitutes the default 10. One code path instead of two means the default can never be applied to the wrong set. The cost is the correlated aggregate, evaluated conceptually once per product, plus the DISTINCT guard. Reach for this whenever the fallback value is the only difference between the two groups - a UNION is better when the branches genuinely compute different things.

solutions.name: ROW_NUMBER Ranking with NOT EXISTS Fallback
solutions.query:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT product_id, new_price,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) AS rn
    FROM Products
    WHERE change_date <= '2019-08-16'
)
SELECT product_id, new_price AS price
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
UNION ALL
SELECT d.product_id, 10 AS price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products) d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Products p
    WHERE p.product_id = d.product_id AND p.change_date <= '2019-08-16'
);
solutions.explanation: This is the ranking mental model: filter the log to changes that have already happened, number each product's changes newest first, and keep number one. It reads more directly than a MAX-and-rejoin because the price travels with the ranked row instead of having to be looked up again, and it extends for free - ask for the two most recent prices and you only change rn = 1 to rn <= 2. ROW_NUMBER also guarantees exactly one winner per product, whereas RANK would return every row tied on change_date, which matters the moment the primary key on (product_id, change_date) is not there to prevent ties. The second branch covers products with no change yet, and NOT EXISTS is used deliberately in place of NOT IN because it is immune to the NULL-in-subquery trap that makes NOT IN return nothing at all.

edgeCases: Products with no changes before or on 2019-08-16: Should correctly return a default price of 10.
Multiple changes before the target date: Must correctly pick the latest change (maximum date).
Changes happening exactly on 2019-08-16: Since the inequality is inclusive (<= '2019-08-16'), these changes must be captured.

Last Person to Fit in the Bus.title: Last Person to Fit in the Bus
Last Person to Fit in the Bus.problemStatement:
There is a queue of people waiting to board a bus. However, the bus has a weight limit of 1000 kilograms, so there may be some people who cannot board.
Write a solution to find the person_name of the last person that can fit on the bus without exceeding the weight limit. The people board the bus in the order of their turn.

solutions.name: Window Function Cumulative Sum
solutions.query:
WITH CumulativeWeight AS (
    SELECT person_name, turn,
           SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn ASC) AS total_weight
    FROM Queue
)
SELECT person_name
FROM CumulativeWeight
WHERE total_weight <= 1000
ORDER BY turn DESC
LIMIT 1;
solutions.explanation: Using the SUM() OVER (ORDER BY turn ASC) window function, we calculate the running total weight of passengers boarding in order of their turns. We then filter out rows where the cumulative weight exceeds 1000. Finally, sorting the remaining passengers by their turn descending and using LIMIT 1 gives us the last passenger who successfully fits.

solutions.name: Self-Join Cumulative Sum
solutions.query:
SELECT q1.person_name
FROM Queue q1
JOIN Queue q2 ON q1.turn >= q2.turn
GROUP BY q1.person_id, q1.person_name, q1.turn
HAVING SUM(q2.weight) <= 1000
ORDER BY q1.turn DESC
LIMIT 1;
solutions.explanation: For compatibility with older SQL database versions without window function support, we can use a self-join. We join the Queue table with itself on q1.turn >= q2.turn to match each passenger with all passengers who board before or at the same turn. Grouping by q1's attributes, we calculate the SUM of weights from q2. We filter groups with a sum <= 1000, sort by turn descending, and limit to 1.

edgeCases: The very first passenger's weight exceeds 1000: The query will return an empty set.
Cumulative weight equals exactly 1000: The filter '<= 1000' correctly includes this limit.
All passengers combined do not exceed 1000: The query will return the person with the maximum turn.

Employees Whose Manager Left the Company.title: Employees Whose Manager Left the Company
Employees Whose Manager Left the Company.problemStatement: The Employees table holds one row per current employee: employee_id as the primary key, name, manager_id pointing at the employee_id of that person's manager, and salary. Departures are handled by deleting the person's row, but the manager_id values that referred to them are left untouched, so a manager_id can point at an employee_id that no longer exists in the table. A manager_id of NULL means the employee simply has no manager and must not be treated as a departure. Return the employee_id of every employee who satisfies both conditions at once: a salary strictly below 30000, and a non-NULL manager_id that matches no surviving row in the table. Output a single employee_id column ordered ascending.

solutions.name: Anti-Join with NOT IN
solutions.query:
SELECT employee_id
FROM Employees
WHERE salary < 30000
  AND manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND manager_id NOT IN (
      SELECT employee_id
      FROM Employees
  )
ORDER BY employee_id;
solutions.explanation: The subquery materialises the set of employee ids that still exist, and NOT IN keeps only the rows whose manager is absent from that set; the salary test is an ordinary row-level filter applied alongside. Two NULL details decide whether this is right or wrong. The explicit 'manager_id IS NOT NULL' is required because a NULL manager_id would make the NOT IN comparison unknown and drop the row anyway — here that happens to be the wanted behaviour, but relying on it is fragile and unreadable. More importantly, NOT IN is only safe because employee_id is the primary key and can never be NULL; if the inner list could contain a single NULL the whole predicate would be unknown for every row and the query would return nothing at all, the most notorious silent failure in SQL.

solutions.name: Anti-Join with NOT EXISTS
solutions.query:
SELECT e.employee_id
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.salary < 30000
  AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM Employees m
      WHERE m.employee_id = e.manager_id
  )
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
solutions.explanation: Same idea, expressed as a correlated existence test against a second alias of the same table: keep the employee when no surviving row carries their manager's id. NOT EXISTS answers strictly true or false, never unknown, so it cannot be sabotaged by NULLs in the inner column the way NOT IN can — this is the version to reach for by default when the key you are probing is nullable or when you are unsure. It also stops at the first match instead of building the whole id list, and with a primary key on employee_id each probe is a single index seek. The self-reference is the thing to notice here: the manager hierarchy lives inside one table, so the alias m is just the same rows viewed as potential managers.

solutions.name: LEFT JOIN and Keep the Unmatched Rows
solutions.query:
SELECT e.employee_id
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary < 30000
  AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND m.employee_id IS NULL
ORDER BY e.employee_id;
solutions.explanation: The self LEFT JOIN tries to attach each employee's manager row; when the manager has been deleted nothing attaches and every m column comes back NULL, so testing 'm.employee_id IS NULL' isolates exactly the orphaned rows. This is the classic anti-join pattern, and it is worth learning because the same join can serve two purposes: remove the IS NULL test and you can select m.name to report who each surviving manager is. Two cautions. The null-check must target a column that is never NULL in a matched row, which is why employee_id and not name is used. And the join predicate must sit in the ON clause, since moving it into WHERE would turn the LEFT JOIN back into an inner join and silently return nothing.

edgeCases: Manager ID is NULL: These employees must not be selected since they don't have a manager. The manager_id IS NOT NULL condition ensures this.
Manager exists but salary is >= 30000: These are excluded by the salary filter.
All managers are active: The query will return an empty result set.

Exchange Seats.title: Exchange Seats
Exchange Seats.problemStatement: The Seat table records a classroom seating chart: id is the seat number and student is the name of the person sitting there. The ids are consecutive integers starting at 1 with no gaps, and id is the primary key. Produce the seating chart after every pair of neighbouring students swaps places: the students in seats 1 and 2 trade, seats 3 and 4 trade, seats 5 and 6 trade, and so on. When the number of students is odd, the person in the final seat has no partner and stays exactly where they are. The output keeps the same two columns, id and student, carries the same set of names as the input, and must be ordered by id ascending - so the answer is really about which name each seat number ends up holding.

solutions.name: Rewrite the Seat Number with CASE
solutions.query:
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN id % 2 = 1 AND id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM Seat) THEN id
        WHEN id % 2 = 1 THEN id + 1
        ELSE id - 1
    END AS id,
    student
FROM Seat
ORDER BY id ASC;
solutions.explanation: Keep each student attached to their name and change the seat number instead. Odd seats move up one, even seats move down one, and the pairing (1,2), (3,4), (5,6) falls straight out of that rule. The single special case is a final odd seat with no partner above it, which the subquery on MAX(id) detects so that student keeps their number. Order matters inside the CASE: SQL takes the first branch that matches, so the 'last odd seat' test has to come before the general odd branch or it would never be reached. Cost is one pass plus one cheap MAX lookup on the primary key. The assumption to be aware of is that ids are consecutive from 1 - with a gap, id + 1 would point at a seat that does not exist and two students could end up sharing a number.

solutions.name: Window Functions (LEAD / LAG)
solutions.query:
SELECT
    id,
    COALESCE(
        CASE
            WHEN id % 2 = 1 THEN LEAD(student) OVER (ORDER BY id)
            ELSE LAG(student)  OVER (ORDER BY id)
        END,
        student
    ) AS student
FROM Seat
ORDER BY id;
solutions.explanation: The mirror image of the first idea: leave the seat numbers alone and pull in the neighbour's name. Ordering by id, an odd seat wants the row after it (LEAD) and an even seat wants the row before it (LAG), which is precisely the swap. The elegance is that it never needs to know the maximum id - LEAD past the last row simply returns NULL, and COALESCE turns that NULL back into the student's own name, handling the odd-sized class as a natural consequence rather than a special case. It also survives gaps in the id sequence, because LEAD and LAG work on row position within the ordering, not on arithmetic over the values. It costs one ordered pass and needs MySQL 8.0 or later; on 5.7 you are back to the CASE version or a self-join.

solutions.name: Self-Join to the Partner Seat
solutions.query:
SELECT s.id,
       COALESCE(p.student, s.student) AS student
FROM Seat s
LEFT JOIN Seat p
       ON p.id = CASE WHEN s.id % 2 = 1 THEN s.id + 1 ELSE s.id - 1 END
ORDER BY s.id;
solutions.explanation: State the relationship directly: every seat has a partner seat, and after the swap a seat shows its partner's student. The CASE inside the ON clause computes that partner id - one up from an odd seat, one down from an even one - and the LEFT JOIN is what makes the odd-class case safe: the final unpaired seat finds no partner row, p.student comes back NULL, and COALESCE falls back to the original occupant. Written as an INNER JOIN that student would vanish from the output entirely, which is the mistake to watch for. This version reads well and runs on any MySQL version, unlike LEAD/LAG, and because the join predicate hits the primary key it is cheap. Like the CASE approach it does assume ids form an unbroken run, since the partner is computed by arithmetic.

edgeCases: Odd number of records: The last record should not be swapped. In the CASE WHEN solution, the check 'id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM Seat)' handles this. In the window function solution, COALESCE handles this.
Only 1 student: Should return that student unchanged.
Table is empty: Returns empty result.

Movie Rating.title: Movie Rating
Movie Rating.problemStatement: Three tables. Movies maps movie_id to a title, Users maps user_id to a name, and MovieRating has one row per (movie_id, user_id) pair holding the rating that user gave that movie and the created_at date on which they gave it. Produce a single one-column result named results containing exactly two rows. The first row is the name of the user who submitted the greatest number of ratings overall, with no date restriction; if several users are tied on count, take the lexicographically smallest name. The second row is the title of the movie with the highest average rating among ratings created in February 2020 only, and again ties are broken by taking the lexicographically smallest title. The user row must come before the movie row, and duplicates must be preserved should the winning name and the winning title ever be identical strings.

solutions.name: UNION ALL of Two ORDER BY / LIMIT Subqueries
solutions.query:
(
    SELECT u.name AS results
    FROM MovieRating r
    JOIN Users u ON u.user_id = r.user_id
    GROUP BY r.user_id, u.name
    ORDER BY COUNT(r.movie_id) DESC, u.name ASC
    LIMIT 1
)
UNION ALL
(
    SELECT m.title AS results
    FROM MovieRating r
    JOIN Movies m ON m.movie_id = r.movie_id
    WHERE r.created_at >= '2020-02-01' AND r.created_at <= '2020-02-29'
    GROUP BY r.movie_id, m.title
    ORDER BY AVG(r.rating) DESC, m.title ASC
    LIMIT 1
);
solutions.explanation: Two unrelated questions share one output shape, so each is solved independently and the answers are stacked. Every tie rule is encoded in the ORDER BY: the primary key of the sort is the metric descending, the secondary key is the name or title ascending, and LIMIT 1 then takes the single winner deterministically. UNION ALL matters more than it looks; plain UNION would deduplicate and collapse the result to one row if the top user and the top movie ever shared a string. The parentheses around each branch are MySQL syntax that lets a branch carry its own ORDER BY and LIMIT, which is exactly what LeetCode grades, though some engines require wrapping each branch in a derived table instead. Reach for this whenever the report is a concatenation of separate answers rather than one computation.

solutions.name: Scalar Subqueries in the Select List
solutions.query:
SELECT (
    SELECT u.name
    FROM MovieRating r
    JOIN Users u ON u.user_id = r.user_id
    GROUP BY r.user_id, u.name
    ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, u.name ASC
    LIMIT 1
) AS results
UNION ALL
SELECT (
    SELECT m.title
    FROM MovieRating r
    JOIN Movies m ON m.movie_id = r.movie_id
    WHERE r.created_at BETWEEN '2020-02-01' AND '2020-02-29'
    GROUP BY r.movie_id, m.title
    ORDER BY AVG(r.rating) DESC, m.title ASC
    LIMIT 1
);
solutions.explanation: Same two computations, but each is evaluated as a scalar subquery producing a single value, and the outer selects contribute one row each with no FROM clause at all. Because the ORDER BY and LIMIT now live safely inside a subquery, the compound statement needs no parenthesised branches, which makes this version portable to engines that reject MySQL's bracketed UNION arms. It also fails loudly in a useful way: if a branch somehow returned more than one row the database raises an error rather than quietly picking one. The subtle risk is the opposite of the first version's, since a branch that matches nothing yields a NULL row instead of no row, so an empty February would still produce two output rows with the second one blank.

solutions.name: CTEs with RANK
solutions.query:
WITH user_counts AS (
    SELECT u.name AS results, COUNT(*) AS rating_count
    FROM MovieRating r
    JOIN Users u ON u.user_id = r.user_id
    GROUP BY r.user_id, u.name
),
feb_movies AS (
    SELECT m.title AS results, AVG(r.rating * 1.0) AS avg_rating
    FROM MovieRating r
    JOIN Movies m ON m.movie_id = r.movie_id
    WHERE r.created_at >= '2020-02-01' AND r.created_at < '2020-03-01'
    GROUP BY r.movie_id, m.title
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT results, 1 AS section,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY rating_count DESC, results ASC) AS rnk
    FROM user_counts
    UNION ALL
    SELECT results, 2 AS section,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY avg_rating DESC, results ASC) AS rnk
    FROM feb_movies
)
SELECT results
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY section;
solutions.explanation: Naming the two intermediate result sets turns a dense query into three readable steps: count per user, average per February movie, then pick the winner of each. Ranking with the tie-break folded into the window's ORDER BY is equivalent to sorting and limiting, but it scales to 'the top three users' by changing one number, and it keeps the metric available if you later want to print it. The explicit section column plus the final ORDER BY is what guarantees the user line comes before the movie line; a bare UNION ALL makes no ordering promise even though it usually looks ordered. Note the date range uses a half-open comparison, which is the habit to build because it stays correct for leap years and for created_at columns that secretly carry a time component.

edgeCases: Ties in number of reviews or average rating: Solved by sorting alphabetically ascending (u.name ASC / m.title ASC).
Rating dates: Correctly check that created_at is within February 2020.
Using UNION ALL instead of UNION: Ensures both parts run independently and two records are output even if the username matches the movie name.

Restaurant Growth.title: Restaurant Growth
